questions.domain: ML Solution Monitoring, Maintenance, and Security
questions.promptHtml: A marine logistics provider's ML platform team uses AWS CodePipeline and AWS CodeBuild to package inference containers, push images to Amazon ECR, and start Amazon SageMaker Pipelines for model validation and deployment. A security review requires the team to remove plaintext credentials from the pipeline, reduce overly broad permissions, and keep build artifacts protected. The team wants to keep the existing CI/CD workflow with minimal redesign. Which action will best meet these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A marine logistics provider's ML platform team uses AWS CodePipeline and AWS CodeBuild to package inference containers, push images to Amazon ECR, and start Amazon SageMaker Pipelines for model validation and deployment. A security review requires the team to remove plaintext credentials from the pipeline, reduce overly broad permissions, and keep build artifacts protected. The team wants to keep the existing CI/CD workflow with minimal redesign.

Which action will best meet these requirements?

options.text: Store secrets as plaintext CodeBuild environment variables, restrict console access to the pipeline, and rotate the variables after each release.
Store secrets in AWS Secrets Manager, encrypt pipeline artifacts with AWS KMS, and scope pipeline service roles to required actions.
Store secrets as encrypted strings in the source repository, enable CloudTrail logging, and grant AdministratorAccess to build roles.
Store secrets in an Amazon S3 artifact bucket, enable bucket versioning, and allow the pipeline role full access to the bucket.

correctText: Store secrets in AWS Secrets Manager, encrypt pipeline artifacts with AWS KMS, and scope pipeline service roles to required actions.
questions.explanationHtml:
Secure ML CI/CD pipelines should treat the pipeline as a privileged production system, not just as developer tooling. Build and deployment automation often has permissions to create containers, read datasets or artifacts, update endpoints, and start SageMaker workflows, so a compromised pipeline can directly affect production models.

The best approach combines least privilege, managed secret storage, and artifact encryption. Sensitive values should be retrieved from a purpose-built service such as AWS Secrets Manager rather than being embedded in pipeline definitions, buildspec files, source code, or action configuration. IAM roles for CodePipeline and CodeBuild should allow only the actions needed, such as reading required artifacts, pushing to the intended ECR repository, and invoking the approved SageMaker workflow.

Encryption of pipeline artifacts with AWS KMS helps protect intermediate build outputs and deployment packages while they are stored in Amazon S3. CloudTrail and CloudWatch are still valuable for audit and monitoring, but they do not replace preventive controls such as removing plaintext secrets and narrowing permissions. See CodePipeline security best practices, Configure server-side encryption for artifacts stored in Amazon S3 for CodePipeline, Data protection in AWS CodeBuild, and Security best practices in IAM.

questions.domain: ML Solution Monitoring, Maintenance, and Security
questions.promptHtml: A regional grocery cooperative's inventory analytics team runs a product demand prediction model on an Amazon SageMaker real-time endpoint. The team needs to detect whether live inference requests are drifting from the feature distributions observed during training. The team also wants notifications when quality deviations occur, with the least amount of custom monitoring code. Which solution will meet these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A regional grocery cooperative's inventory analytics team runs a product demand prediction model on an Amazon SageMaker real-time endpoint. The team needs to detect whether live inference requests are drifting from the feature distributions observed during training. The team also wants notifications when quality deviations occur, with the least amount of custom monitoring code.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Create CloudWatch alarms for endpoint invocations, latency, and CPU utilization, and notify the team when operational thresholds change.
Enable endpoint data capture, create a baseline from training data, and schedule monitoring jobs that publish drift violations to CloudWatch.
Enable CloudTrail Insights for SageMaker API activity, and route unusual account write events to EventBridge for notification.
Track model versions in SageMaker Experiments, and compare training trial metrics before approving the next endpoint deployment.

correctText: Enable endpoint data capture, create a baseline from training data, and schedule monitoring jobs that publish drift violations to CloudWatch.
questions.explanationHtml:
Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor is the managed service designed for this kind of production inference monitoring. A common pattern is to enable data capture on a SageMaker endpoint, store captured inference inputs and outputs in Amazon S3, create a baseline from representative training or validation data, and run scheduled monitoring jobs that compare current traffic with that baseline. For more detail, see Monitor data and model quality with Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor and Capture data from deployed models.

CloudWatch remains part of the solution, but it plays a different role. CloudWatch endpoint metrics are appropriate for monitoring operational behavior, such as invocation rates, latency, errors, and resource utilization, while Model Monitor provides the ML-specific comparison against baselines and can publish metrics or violations for alarming. See Monitor Amazon SageMaker with Amazon CloudWatch and Monitor data quality.

CloudTrail and CloudTrail Insights are governance and audit tools for API activity in an AWS account, not tools for inspecting model inputs and outputs. SageMaker Experiments is useful during development for comparing training runs, but it does not replace runtime monitoring of deployed inference traffic.

questions.domain: Deployment and Orchestration of ML Workflows
questions.promptHtml: A renewable energy trading desk's ML engineering team trained a custom PyTorch price-forecasting model. The model artifacts are stored in Amazon S3, and the inference code is available in a container image. The team needs to deploy a persistent endpoint for low-latency validation requests from a notebook before promoting the model. The team wants to define deployment settings in Python code and avoid maintaining infrastructure templates for this validation step. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
questions.promptText:
A renewable energy trading desk's ML engineering team trained a custom PyTorch price-forecasting model. The model artifacts are stored in Amazon S3, and the inference code is available in a container image. The team needs to deploy a persistent endpoint for low-latency validation requests from a notebook before promoting the model. The team wants to define deployment settings in Python code and avoid maintaining infrastructure templates for this validation step.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Use the SageMaker Python SDK to build the model object and call deploy to create a real-time endpoint.
Use SageMaker batch transform to process validation records and write prediction output to Amazon S3.
Use AWS CloudFormation to define SageMaker model, endpoint configuration, and endpoint resources for validation.
Use SageMaker JumpStart to select a pretrained model and deploy it to a preconfigured real-time endpoint.

correctText: Use the SageMaker Python SDK to build the model object and call deploy to create a real-time endpoint.
questions.explanationHtml:
For a custom model that is already trained and stored as artifacts, Amazon SageMaker AI real-time inference is the deployment pattern for persistent, low-latency request and response validation. The SageMaker Python SDK provides a practical developer workflow from a notebook: define the model and deployment settings in code, deploy an endpoint, then use a predictor or endpoint invocation to run smoke tests.

The key tradeoff is between developer velocity and deployment governance. For notebook-based validation, the SDK avoids the extra work of writing CloudFormation resources while still creating the SageMaker model, endpoint configuration, and endpoint resources behind the scenes. CloudFormation is better suited when the team needs fully repeatable infrastructure as code for production promotion or regulated release pipelines.

SageMaker JumpStart is optimized for quickly deploying pretrained models from a catalog, not for substituting a team's already trained custom model. Batch transform is a different inference mode, it processes datasets asynchronously and stores results, rather than keeping an endpoint available for interactive validation requests.

For more information, see High-level SageMaker AI deployment options, Real-time endpoint deployment workflow, and ModelBuilder guide.

questions.domain: Deployment and Orchestration of ML Workflows
questions.promptHtml: A national weather analytics provider's forecast operations team hosts a custom PyTorch model on an Amazon SageMaker real-time endpoint. The endpoint meets its latency SLA, but utilization is low and the monthly cost is higher than expected. The team has a short list of candidate CPU instance types and wants to compare cost, latency, and throughput under expected traffic patterns without building a custom load-testing framework. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational effort?
questions.promptText:
A national weather analytics provider's forecast operations team hosts a custom PyTorch model on an Amazon SageMaker real-time endpoint. The endpoint meets its latency SLA, but utilization is low and the monthly cost is higher than expected. The team has a short list of candidate CPU instance types and wants to compare cost, latency, and throughput under expected traffic patterns without building a custom load-testing framework.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational effort?

options.text: Move the model to a SageMaker serverless endpoint, and compare CloudWatch invocation metrics after shifting production traffic to the new endpoint.
Deploy the model to a larger GPU-backed real-time endpoint, and enable Application Auto Scaling before comparing latency during production traffic.
Register the model in SageMaker Model Registry, and run a SageMaker Inference Recommender endpoint recommendation job with the candidate instances and traffic requirements.
Run SageMaker Batch Transform on a recent request sample, and compare total job duration across the candidate instance types.

correctText: Register the model in SageMaker Model Registry, and run a SageMaker Inference Recommender endpoint recommendation job with the candidate instances and traffic requirements.
questions.explanationHtml:
SageMaker Inference Recommender is the best fit when an ML team needs evidence-based guidance for hosting a model with the right balance of performance and cost. It can benchmark endpoint configurations and produce metrics that help compare instance choices instead of relying on guesswork or manual load-test scripts. The course material distinguishes quick instance recommendations from more customized endpoint recommendations, where the team specifies candidate instances, traffic patterns, latency requirements, and throughput requirements.

Serverless Inference is useful when traffic is intermittent or uneven and the workload can tolerate cold starts, but it is a deployment mode, not the most direct way to evaluate several CPU endpoint configurations before a change. Real-time endpoints with auto scaling are appropriate for low-latency interactive workloads, but auto scaling adjusts capacity after the instance family is chosen. Batch Transform is a separate offline inference pattern for processing datasets, so it does not answer whether a production endpoint will satisfy request latency and throughput targets.

For more information, see Amazon SageMaker Inference Recommender, Optimize your inference costs, and Real-time inference.

questions.promptHtml: A telemedicine provider's ML team trains an Amazon SageMaker built-in XGBoost binary classification model to predict appointment no-shows. The model has high performance on the training dataset but substantially lower performance on the validation dataset. The team observes that the boosted trees are becoming overly complex and wants to make a hyperparameter change that directly limits the complexity of each tree while keeping the same algorithm and dataset. Which action will best meet this requirement?
questions.promptText:
A telemedicine provider's ML team trains an Amazon SageMaker built-in XGBoost binary classification model to predict appointment no-shows. The model has high performance on the training dataset but substantially lower performance on the validation dataset. The team observes that the boosted trees are becoming overly complex and wants to make a hyperparameter change that directly limits the complexity of each tree while keeping the same algorithm and dataset.

Which action will best meet this requirement?

options.text: Increase the max_depth hyperparameter to capture more feature interactions in each boosted tree.
Increase the num_round hyperparameter to add more boosting iterations during training.
Change the eval_metric hyperparameter to report a different validation metric during training.
Reduce the max_depth hyperparameter to constrain how deep each boosted tree can grow.

correctText: Reduce the max_depth hyperparameter to constrain how deep each boosted tree can grow.
questions.explanationHtml:
In XGBoost, model capacity is strongly affected by tree-structure hyperparameters. The max_depth hyperparameter limits how deep each boosted tree can grow, so lowering it is a direct way to make each tree simpler and reduce the risk that the model memorizes training-specific patterns. This is a common response when the model performs well on training data but much worse on validation data, which is a classic sign of overfitting.

Other hyperparameters affect training in different ways. Increasing num_round usually gives the model more boosting iterations, which can increase capacity if not controlled by early stopping or other regularization. Changing eval_metric can change how training progress is measured, but it does not by itself reduce tree complexity. SageMaker automatic model tuning can search over hyperparameter ranges and select the best training job based on an objective metric, but the engineer still needs to understand which hyperparameters affect model complexity. For more information, see SageMaker XGBoost hyperparameters and SageMaker AI Automatic Model Tuning overview.

questions.domain: ML Solution Monitoring, Maintenance, and Security
questions.promptHtml: A digital advertising analytics team runs a nightly Spark feature-engineering workload on Amazon EMR before training a recommendation model. The cluster reads raw logs from Amazon S3 and writes curated features back to S3. The team uses HDFS only for intermediate processing data and must reduce compute cost while avoiding unnecessary risk to the cluster's storage and coordination roles. Which purchasing strategy should the team use for the EMR cluster?
questions.promptText:
A digital advertising analytics team runs a nightly Spark feature-engineering workload on Amazon EMR before training a recommendation model. The cluster reads raw logs from Amazon S3 and writes curated features back to S3. The team uses HDFS only for intermediate processing data and must reduce compute cost while avoiding unnecessary risk to the cluster's storage and coordination roles.

Which purchasing strategy should the team use for the EMR cluster?

options.text: Run the entire EMR cluster on On-Demand Instances, and rely on AWS Budgets alerts for cost control.
Purchase Reserved Instances for the task node fleet, and keep master and core nodes on On-Demand Instances.
Run the master and core node groups on On-Demand Instances, and add Spot Instances only as task nodes.
Run the master, core, and task node groups on Spot Instances, and increase HDFS replication settings.

correctText: Run the master and core node groups on On-Demand Instances, and add Spot Instances only as task nodes.
questions.explanationHtml:
For Amazon EMR clusters, the node role matters when selecting a purchasing option. Master nodes coordinate the cluster, core nodes run tasks and store data in HDFS, and task nodes run tasks without storing HDFS data. Because task nodes are optional compute capacity, they are a good place to use lower-cost Spot Instances when the workload can tolerate task interruption or retry.

Using Spot Instances for master or core nodes is a common cost anti-pattern unless the workload is experimental or the team is extremely cost sensitive. If a core node that stores HDFS blocks is interrupted, the cluster can be exposed to partial data loss or job disruption. Keeping master and core nodes on On-Demand Instances preserves stability while still reducing cost by adding Spot capacity for task nodes.

AWS Budgets is useful for alerts and governance, but it does not itself choose cheaper capacity. Reserved Instances and Savings Plans are better aligned with sustained, predictable usage commitments, while Spot Instances are designed for spare capacity that can be interrupted. For purchasing option comparisons, see Amazon EC2 instance purchasing options and Amazon EC2 Spot Instances.

questions.domain: Deployment and Orchestration of ML Workflows
questions.promptHtml: A precision agriculture drone manufacturer's ML team trained a custom image classification model in Amazon SageMaker. The team is preparing a real-time inference endpoint and is unsure whether CPU instances will meet the latency target or whether GPU instances are needed. The team wants to compare candidate endpoint configurations under expected traffic before choosing production compute resources. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST custom testing effort?
questions.promptText:
A precision agriculture drone manufacturer's ML team trained a custom image classification model in Amazon SageMaker. The team is preparing a real-time inference endpoint and is unsure whether CPU instances will meet the latency target or whether GPU instances are needed. The team wants to compare candidate endpoint configurations under expected traffic before choosing production compute resources.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST custom testing effort?

options.text: Enable SageMaker Training Compiler on a GPU training job and use the compiled training result to choose the endpoint instance type.
Create SageMaker Processing jobs on candidate CPU and GPU instances and compare CloudWatch utilization metrics from each processing job.
Register the model in SageMaker Model Registry and run a SageMaker Inference Recommender endpoint recommendation job with candidate CPU and GPU instances.
Deploy the model to two SageMaker production variants and split live traffic evenly across candidate CPU and GPU instances.

correctText: Register the model in SageMaker Model Registry and run a SageMaker Inference Recommender endpoint recommendation job with candidate CPU and GPU instances.
questions.explanationHtml:
SageMaker Inference Recommender is designed for the decision point in this scenario: selecting an inference instance type and endpoint configuration based on measured behavior instead of guesswork. The course material describes two modes: instance recommendations, which run load tests on recommended instance types, and endpoint recommendations, which use a custom load test where you specify candidate instances, traffic patterns, latency requirements, and throughput requirements.

For production hosting, SageMaker defines compute resources through endpoint configurations and production variants. A production variant includes resources such as the hosting instance type and initial instance count, and it can also be used for traffic splitting once a deployment strategy has been chosen. The relevant documentation describes endpoint configurations in CreateEndpointConfig and production variant resource settings in ProductionVariant.

Splitting live traffic between variants can be useful for A/B testing, but it is not the least-risk way to answer an initial CPU versus GPU sizing question. Processing jobs and training optimizations also solve different problems: processing jobs run data processing or evaluation code, and Training Compiler optimizes certain training workloads. For inference capacity planning, the better mental model is to benchmark the serving path, including model container startup, request handling, latency, throughput, and cost per inference, before selecting the endpoint compute.

For more context, see the SageMaker guidance on Test models in production and the training compute overview in Train a Model with Amazon SageMaker.

questions.promptHtml: A museum consortium's digital archives team stores visitor survey exports in Amazon S3. The exports include names, email addresses, and free-form comments. Data stewards need a visual workflow to profile the data, apply repeatable transformations that mask or delete personally identifiable information, and run the transformations as a managed job that writes cleaned datasets back to Amazon S3. The team wants to avoid writing Spark code or maintaining processing clusters. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
questions.promptText:
A museum consortium's digital archives team stores visitor survey exports in Amazon S3. The exports include names, email addresses, and free-form comments. Data stewards need a visual workflow to profile the data, apply repeatable transformations that mask or delete personally identifiable information, and run the transformations as a managed job that writes cleaned datasets back to Amazon S3. The team wants to avoid writing Spark code or maintaining processing clusters.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Use AWS Glue Studio to create a visual ETL job, add managed transform nodes, and run the job on AWS Glue Spark infrastructure.
Use Apache Spark on Amazon EMR to run a PySpark script that profiles the files, masks PII fields, and writes output to Amazon S3.
Use SageMaker Data Wrangler to import the dataset, add built-in transformations, and export the prepared data flow to a processing job.
Use AWS Glue DataBrew to profile the dataset, build a transformation recipe, and run a recipe job that writes output to Amazon S3.

correctText: Use AWS Glue DataBrew to profile the dataset, build a transformation recipe, and run a recipe job that writes output to Amazon S3.
questions.explanationHtml:
AWS Glue DataBrew is the best match when the work is primarily visual data preparation, profiling, and repeatable cleansing rather than custom distributed engineering. DataBrew lets users define ordered transformation steps as recipes, including transformations for masking, hashing, encryption, deletion, and other PII handling patterns covered in the course material. Those recipes can then be run as managed jobs and written back to destinations such as Amazon S3, which fits a stewardship workflow that should not require Spark development.

AWS Glue Studio is also a visual ETL tool, but it is centered on Glue ETL jobs and Spark-style data integration. It is a strong choice for general ETL pipelines, especially when engineers need DAG-style workflows, joins, and transforms across sources, but it is not the lowest-overhead choice for non-coding stewards who need profiling and reusable PII cleansing recipes. Amazon EMR with Spark is powerful for large-scale transformations, but it introduces code and cluster lifecycle concerns that the scenario explicitly wants to avoid.

SageMaker Data Wrangler is highly relevant for ML feature preparation in SageMaker Studio, including visual transformations and export to SageMaker processing or pipelines. In this scenario, however, the core requirement is governed data cleansing and PII handling for S3 datasets rather than preparing features inside a SageMaker ML workflow. For more information, see AWS Glue DataBrew recipes, AWS Glue DataBrew recipe jobs, AWS Glue Studio managed transform nodes, Apache Spark on Amazon EMR, and SageMaker Data Wrangler transform data.

questions.promptHtml: A biomedical device manufacturer's ML team trains a PyTorch convolutional model on tens of millions of labeled sensor images by using Amazon SageMaker. The model fits in GPU memory on a single instance, but each training run takes too long because the dataset is large. The team wants to reduce wall clock training time by using multiple GPU instances while preserving the model architecture. Which solution is most appropriate?
questions.promptText:
A biomedical device manufacturer's ML team trains a PyTorch convolutional model on tens of millions of labeled sensor images by using Amazon SageMaker. The model fits in GPU memory on a single instance, but each training run takes too long because the dataset is large. The team wants to reduce wall clock training time by using multiple GPU instances while preserving the model architecture.

Which solution is most appropriate?

options.text: Increase the number of parallel automatic model tuning jobs, use random search, and compare more hyperparameter combinations at once.
Enable SageMaker Training Compiler, keep the existing distributed training configuration, and compile the model on GPU instances.
Enable SageMaker Distributed Data Parallel, initialize PyTorch with the smddp backend, and run the training job across multiple GPU instances.
Enable SageMaker model parallelism, shard the model layers across GPUs, and keep the same dataset on each training instance.

correctText: Enable SageMaker Distributed Data Parallel, initialize PyTorch with the smddp backend, and run the training job across multiple GPU instances.
questions.explanationHtml:
When a training job is slow because the dataset is large and the model already fits on a single GPU, the usual distributed training pattern is data parallelism. Each worker processes a different slice of each batch, computes gradients, and synchronizes updates so the model learns as if it were training on the combined data. SageMaker provides distributed training libraries for this pattern, including PyTorch integration that can use the smddp backend, as described in SageMaker distributed training and Get started with distributed training.

Model parallelism solves a different problem: the model itself is too large for one device, or the team wants to partition model state and activations across GPUs. That adds communication and implementation overhead, so it is not the best first choice when the architecture already fits in memory. Training Compiler and automatic model tuning can reduce training cost or improve model quality in other situations, but they do not directly match the stated need to distribute one PyTorch training run across multiple GPU instances. For early stopping in tuning jobs, see Use early stopping.

questions.promptHtml: A public library network's digital services team is preparing training data for three supervised ML models: a tabular model that predicts overdue account risk, a text classifier that routes patron support messages, and an image classifier that identifies damaged returned materials. Data profiling shows class imbalance in each dataset, with valid minority-class examples that are much rarer than majority-class examples. The team cannot collect enough new real-world examples before the next training cycle and wants to preserve as much existing data as possible. Which TWO actions should the team take to address the imbalance before training?
questions.promptText:
A public library network's digital services team is preparing training data for three supervised ML models: a tabular model that predicts overdue account risk, a text classifier that routes patron support messages, and an image classifier that identifies damaged returned materials. Data profiling shows class imbalance in each dataset, with valid minority-class examples that are much rarer than majority-class examples. The team cannot collect enough new real-world examples before the next training cycle and wants to preserve as much existing data as possible.

Which TWO actions should the team take to address the imbalance before training?

options.text: Apply random oversampling to the majority classes to preserve the original class distribution.
Apply random undersampling to remove minority-class examples from each training dataset.
Generate label-preserving augmented examples for minority-class text and image records before training.
Apply random oversampling or SMOTE to increase minority-class representation in the tabular dataset.
Run a SageMaker Clarify CI report after training and keep the training data unchanged.

correctText: Generate label-preserving augmented examples for minority-class text and image records before training.
Apply random oversampling or SMOTE to increase minority-class representation in the tabular dataset.
questions.explanationHtml:
Class Imbalance (CI) means that one class or facet has fewer examples than another. In supervised learning, this often causes the model to learn majority-class patterns well while performing poorly on the minority class, even when overall accuracy looks acceptable. SageMaker Clarify includes a CI metric for identifying this kind of imbalance before training, as described in Class Imbalance and the broader pre-training bias metrics documentation.

When the team wants to preserve existing data, oversampling and synthetic data generation are usually better fits than removing data. For tabular numeric data, random oversampling duplicates minority examples, while SMOTE creates synthetic minority examples from neighboring samples. SageMaker Data Wrangler documents balance-data approaches such as random oversampling, random undersampling, and SMOTE in Transform data.

For image and text datasets, label-preserving augmentation can increase minority-class coverage when new labeled data is hard to obtain. Image augmentation might create transformed versions that retain the same label, while text augmentation must be handled carefully so that meaning and label are preserved. For image workloads, SageMaker image classification documentation includes augmentation-related options in Image Classification hyperparameters.

Undersampling can be useful only when it removes majority-class examples in a controlled way, and it trades lower imbalance for less training data. Removing minority examples, oversampling majority examples, or only measuring CI without changing the dataset fails to address the root problem.

questions.promptHtml: An insurance actuarial modeling team runs repeated Amazon SageMaker training jobs to test different feature transformations and hyperparameter settings for a claims severity model. The team must be able to compare experiment results, reproduce the workflow that produced a selected model, and maintain an auditable record of the datasets and model artifacts that were used. The team wants to minimize custom tracking code. Which TWO actions should the team take? (Select TWO.)
questions.promptText:
An insurance actuarial modeling team runs repeated Amazon SageMaker training jobs to test different feature transformations and hyperparameter settings for a claims severity model. The team must be able to compare experiment results, reproduce the workflow that produced a selected model, and maintain an auditable record of the datasets and model artifacts that were used. The team wants to minimize custom tracking code.

Which TWO actions should the team take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Use Amazon QuickSight dashboards to visualize validation metrics and select the highest scoring run.
Use SageMaker Pipelines with Model Registry and ML Lineage Tracking for repeatable training workflows.
Use date-stamped Amazon S3 folders for notebooks and rerun the latest notebook manually.
Use SageMaker Experiments to track runs, parameters, metrics, and artifacts for each training attempt.
Use CloudWatch Logs Insights to query training logs and save dashboard queries for each run.

correctText: Use SageMaker Pipelines with Model Registry and ML Lineage Tracking for repeatable training workflows.
Use SageMaker Experiments to track runs, parameters, metrics, and artifacts for each training attempt.
questions.explanationHtml:
Reproducible ML development requires more than saving a final model file. Engineers need to preserve the context that produced the model: input data, transformations, training parameters, metrics, code path, and resulting artifacts. SageMaker Experiments addresses the comparison side of this problem by helping teams organize trials and evaluate how different feature transformations, algorithms, or hyperparameters affected results. For related managed experiment tracking capabilities, see Track experiments with MLflow.

SageMaker Pipelines addresses the workflow side by turning the training and evaluation process into a repeatable managed workflow instead of a sequence of ad hoc notebook cells. Combining pipelines with Model Registry and ML Lineage Tracking gives the team a stronger audit trail for model versions and the datasets, jobs, parameters, and artifacts connected to them. CloudWatch Logs Insights and QuickSight are useful supporting tools for operational log analysis and visualization, but they do not replace experiment tracking, workflow orchestration, or lineage. Date-stamped folders are a common anti-pattern because they rely on manual discipline rather than managed metadata and reproducible execution. See Amazon SageMaker Pipelines, Amazon SageMaker ML Lineage Tracking, and Register and deploy models with Model Registry.

questions.promptHtml: A professional sports league's fan engagement analytics team receives continuous JSON clickstream events from mobile apps and venue kiosks. The team needs to store the events in an Amazon S3 data lake for later ML feature exploration with SQL-based tools. The team does not need to replay records after delivery. The team wants the lowest operational overhead for ingestion, buffering, basic transformation, and schema discovery. Which TWO steps will meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)
questions.promptText:
A professional sports league's fan engagement analytics team receives continuous JSON clickstream events from mobile apps and venue kiosks. The team needs to store the events in an Amazon S3 data lake for later ML feature exploration with SQL-based tools. The team does not need to replay records after delivery. The team wants the lowest operational overhead for ingestion, buffering, basic transformation, and schema discovery.

Which TWO steps will meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Deploy Amazon Kinesis Data Streams and build consumers to write events to Amazon S3.
Create an Amazon MSK cluster and write Kafka consumers to persist events to Amazon S3.
Configure Amazon Data Firehose to deliver the event stream to Amazon S3.
Run an AWS Glue crawler on the Amazon S3 data lake prefixes.
Use Amazon Athena as the primary service to ingest and transform streaming events.

correctText: Configure Amazon Data Firehose to deliver the event stream to Amazon S3.
Run an AWS Glue crawler on the Amazon S3 data lake prefixes.
questions.explanationHtml:
Amazon Data Firehose is designed for managed streaming ingestion into storage and analytics destinations. It reduces operational work because it handles delivery, buffering, scaling, and optional record transformation before data lands in Amazon S3. This fits a data lake ingestion pattern when the team wants near real-time delivery but does not require the replay model of a stream processing platform. See Amazon Data Firehose overview.

After the data is stored in Amazon S3, the team still needs metadata so SQL-based tools can understand the data layout. An AWS Glue crawler can inspect S3 locations, infer schemas, and populate the AWS Glue Data Catalog, which services such as Athena can use for querying. See AWS Glue crawlers and Amazon S3 fundamentals.

Kinesis Data Streams and Amazon MSK are plausible streaming choices, but they are better suited when the workload needs custom stream processing, consumer applications, Kafka compatibility, or replay behavior. Those capabilities are valuable tradeoffs, but they add engineering work that is not justified by this scenario. Athena is also commonly used with S3 data lakes, but it is a query engine rather than the component that continuously ingests event streams.

questions.domain: ML Solution Monitoring, Maintenance, and Security
questions.promptHtml: A maritime logistics carrier's ML platform team trains Amazon SageMaker models on sensitive customs document features stored in Amazon S3. The security team requires the training environment to run without direct internet access and to access only an approved S3 bucket for training data and model artifacts. The solution must use network isolation controls in the VPC while allowing the training job to complete. Which solution will meet these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A maritime logistics carrier's ML platform team trains Amazon SageMaker models on sensitive customs document features stored in Amazon S3. The security team requires the training environment to run without direct internet access and to access only an approved S3 bucket for training data and model artifacts. The solution must use network isolation controls in the VPC while allowing the training job to complete.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Configure the training job with network isolation enabled and no VPC endpoints. Add an IAM role that allows access to the approved bucket.
Configure the training job with private VPC subnets and a NAT gateway route. Add unrestricted outbound rules and CloudTrail auditing for the bucket.
Configure the training job with private VPC subnets and restrictive security groups. Add an Amazon S3 VPC endpoint with endpoint and bucket policies for the approved bucket.
Configure the training job with public VPC subnets and restrictive security groups. Add an internet gateway route and bucket policies for the approved bucket.

correctText: Configure the training job with private VPC subnets and restrictive security groups. Add an Amazon S3 VPC endpoint with endpoint and bucket policies for the approved bucket.
questions.explanationHtml:
For a secure SageMaker training setup, think of the VPC as the network boundary, the subnet as the placement choice, and the security group as the workload-level firewall. SageMaker training jobs can be configured with specific VPC subnets and security groups so the training containers are attached to the intended private network rather than using a default internet-enabled path. The SageMaker documentation describes this pattern in Give SageMaker Training Jobs Access to Resources in Your Amazon VPC and Give SageMaker Jobs Access to Resources in Your Amazon VPC.

Because the training data and artifacts are in Amazon S3, the private subnet design still needs a private route to S3 when the requirement is to use VPC network controls for S3 access. An Amazon S3 VPC endpoint provides that path without requiring the training environment to reach S3 through the public internet, and policies on the endpoint and bucket help narrow access to the approved bucket. Security groups should be scoped to the traffic the training containers actually need, following the same least-privilege mindset described for security groups in Control Traffic to Resources Using Security Groups.

Using public subnets or a NAT gateway can be valid in other architectures, but those choices conflict with a requirement for no direct internet access. SageMaker network isolation is useful when you need to prevent the training container from making outbound network calls, but by itself it is not the same as placing the job in private VPC subnets with security groups and endpoint policy controls. Subnet placement and subnet-level controls are foundational VPC design decisions, as summarized in Amazon VPC Basics and Configure Subnets.

questions.promptHtml: An energy retailer's demand forecasting team trains a PyTorch neural network in Amazon SageMaker. The training script emits the validation RMSE after each epoch. The team runs automatic model tuning every week, but random search is consuming too many training hours without consistent gains. The team can tolerate some parallel training, but wants to reduce wasted trials and avoid tuning unimportant hyperparameters while preserving model quality. Which approach best meets these requirements?
questions.promptText:
An energy retailer's demand forecasting team trains a PyTorch neural network in Amazon SageMaker. The training script emits the validation RMSE after each epoch. The team runs automatic model tuning every week, but random search is consuming too many training hours without consistent gains. The team can tolerate some parallel training, but wants to reduce wasted trials and avoid tuning unimportant hyperparameters while preserving model quality.

Which approach best meets these requirements?

options.text: Configure SageMaker automatic model tuning to use grid search, and include every available hyperparameter in the search space.
Configure SageMaker automatic model tuning to use Hyperband with early stopping, and tune only the highest-impact hyperparameters.
Replace the single training job with SageMaker distributed data parallel training, and keep manual tuning outside automatic model tuning.
Increase the maximum number of parallel random-search training jobs, and keep the current hyperparameter search space.

correctText: Configure SageMaker automatic model tuning to use Hyperband with early stopping, and tune only the highest-impact hyperparameters.
questions.explanationHtml:
Hyperparameter tuning is a tradeoff between exploring enough configurations to improve the objective metric and avoiding training jobs that are unlikely to pay off. For iterative training workloads, such as neural networks that report a validation metric after each epoch, Hyperband can use early results to stop poor trials and focus resources on more promising configurations. This is why it is a better fit than simply adding more parallel random trials when the goal is to improve both training efficiency and model quality.

Search space design matters as much as the tuning algorithm. Tuning every possible hyperparameter can cause the number of combinations to grow quickly, which increases cost and can make it harder to find useful improvements. A practical ML engineer should focus automatic tuning on the hyperparameters that are most likely to affect the objective metric, then use completion limits or early stopping behavior to control resource usage.

Grid search is usually the least efficient choice in this scenario because it is brute force and does not learn from previous trials. Random search is more parallelizable, but it still wastes work when the search space is too broad. Distributed training addresses the speed of individual training jobs, not the quality or efficiency of hyperparameter selection, and it can add overhead that is not justified if the main bottleneck is poor trial selection.

For more information, see Overview of SageMaker Automatic Model Tuning and How SageMaker Automatic Model Tuning works.

questions.promptHtml: A regional airline's predictive maintenance team receives daily CSV files in Amazon S3 from aircraft maintenance systems. Before the files are used for feature engineering, the team must validate recurring checks such as missing values, unexpected values, and duplicate records. Data analysts need a visual, managed workflow with minimal custom code and repeatable validation results for each dataset refresh. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
questions.promptText:
A regional airline's predictive maintenance team receives daily CSV files in Amazon S3 from aircraft maintenance systems. Before the files are used for feature engineering, the team must validate recurring checks such as missing values, unexpected values, and duplicate records. Data analysts need a visual, managed workflow with minimal custom code and repeatable validation results for each dataset refresh.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Create a SageMaker Model Monitor schedule, build a production baseline, and review drift alerts after deployment.
Create an AWS Glue DataBrew project, define a data quality ruleset, and run DataBrew profile jobs for each refresh.
Create an Amazon QuickSight analysis, add anomaly visuals, and review dashboards after each refresh.
Create an Amazon Macie discovery job, inspect sensitive data findings, and approve files with no alerts.

correctText: Create an AWS Glue DataBrew project, define a data quality ruleset, and run DataBrew profile jobs for each refresh.
questions.explanationHtml:
AWS Glue DataBrew is designed for visual data preparation and profiling, which makes it a strong fit when analysts need to inspect and validate datasets without writing custom ETL code. A DataBrew ruleset can be associated with a dataset and evaluated as part of a profile job, so the team can repeat the same validation checks each time new files arrive.

The important mental model is that data quality validation happens before training. Validating missing values, unexpected values, duplicates, and similar issues helps prevent poor feature engineering decisions and reduces the chance that a model learns from corrupted or misleading data.

QuickSight can help users explore and visualize data, but using dashboards as a quality gate is an anti-pattern when the requirement is repeatable validation. Macie focuses on sensitive data discovery rather than general dataset correctness. SageMaker Model Monitor is valuable after deployment, but it monitors live model inputs and outputs relative to baselines rather than profiling raw training files before they enter the ML pipeline.

For more information, see AWS Glue DataBrew data quality validation and Creating a data quality ruleset in AWS Glue DataBrew.

questions.promptHtml: A university neuroscience lab is preparing a large collection of experiment files for ML training. The files already reside on an Amazon EFS file system that is mounted by several preprocessing applications. The lab wants Amazon SageMaker training jobs to read the same files without first copying the dataset to Amazon S3. The training jobs can run inside the lab's VPC. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST data movement?
questions.promptText:
A university neuroscience lab is preparing a large collection of experiment files for ML training. The files already reside on an Amazon EFS file system that is mounted by several preprocessing applications. The lab wants Amazon SageMaker training jobs to read the same files without first copying the dataset to Amazon S3. The training jobs can run inside the lab's VPC.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST data movement?

options.text: Configure S3 Fast File mode for the training job and reference the Amazon EFS mount path.
Configure the SageMaker training job to use the Amazon EFS file system as the training data source.
Copy the dataset to Amazon S3 and configure the SageMaker training job to use S3 File mode.
Migrate the dataset to Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP and mount it from the SageMaker training job.

correctText: Configure the SageMaker training job to use the Amazon EFS file system as the training data source.
questions.explanationHtml:
Amazon EFS is a shared, elastic file system that can be mounted by multiple clients in a VPC, which makes it a good fit when preprocessing applications and training jobs need to work from the same file tree. In SageMaker training, EFS is appropriate when the dataset is already in EFS and the training job is configured to run with VPC access. This avoids a separate data-copy step to Amazon S3, which is useful when the requirement is minimizing data movement rather than optimizing for an S3-native training workflow.

Amazon S3 remains the most common storage source for SageMaker training and supports input modes such as File mode, Fast File mode, and Pipe mode. However, those modes are S3-oriented and do not turn an EFS path into an S3 source. Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP is a strong choice when an organization needs managed ONTAP capabilities, multiprotocol access, or migration of existing NetApp/NAS workflows, but introducing it here would move data away from the storage service that already satisfies the requirement. For more details, see Access Training Data in SageMaker AI, What is Amazon Elastic File System?, and What is Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP?.

questions.promptHtml: A subscription fitness app's ML team stores monthly CSV exports in Amazon S3 for churn model training. The exports contain email addresses and phone numbers that are needed only to join records across months. Analysts must not access the plaintext values, and the prepared output must keep the same transformed value for the same original value so joins still work. The team wants a repeatable visual data preparation approach with minimal custom code. Which solution will meet these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A subscription fitness app's ML team stores monthly CSV exports in Amazon S3 for churn model training. The exports contain email addresses and phone numbers that are needed only to join records across months. Analysts must not access the plaintext values, and the prepared output must keep the same transformed value for the same original value so joins still work. The team wants a repeatable visual data preparation approach with minimal custom code.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Configure Amazon Macie sensitive data discovery on the S3 bucket, then review findings before granting analysts access.
Apply AWS Lake Formation LF-Tags to classify the tables, then grant analysts tag-based access to the restricted columns.
Run an AWS Glue DataBrew profile job with PII statistics, then apply probabilistic encryption in a recipe to the PII columns.
Run an AWS Glue DataBrew profile job with PII statistics, then apply deterministic encryption in a recipe to the PII columns.

correctText: Run an AWS Glue DataBrew profile job with PII statistics, then apply deterministic encryption in a recipe to the PII columns.
questions.explanationHtml:
AWS Glue DataBrew is designed for visual, repeatable data preparation, including PII identification and protection steps. In this scenario, the important nuance is not only hiding email addresses and phone numbers, but also keeping a stable replacement value so records from different months can still be joined. A DataBrew profile job can help identify PII, and a recipe can apply transformations such as masking, hashing, or encryption before writing prepared data back to Amazon S3.

Deterministic encryption is the best match when equality must be preserved after obfuscation, because the same original value can be transformed consistently. Probabilistic encryption is useful when stronger non-repeatability is desired, but that property works against the join requirement. Amazon Macie helps classify and alert on sensitive data in S3, but it is not the transformation step that produces a sanitized ML-ready dataset. Lake Formation LF-Tags are useful for governance and access control, but tagging or restricting access is different from anonymizing values for model development.

For more information, see AWS Glue DataBrew personal information protection, Amazon Macie sensitive data discovery, and AWS Lake Formation tag-based access control.

questions.promptHtml: An online grocery retailer's personalization team hosts a recommendation model on an Amazon SageMaker real-time endpoint. The team has trained a replacement model and wants to compare the replacement model against the current model by using live request patterns. The replacement model must not return responses to customers until the team confirms that its prediction behavior and latency are acceptable. Which solution will meet these requirements?
questions.promptText:
An online grocery retailer's personalization team hosts a recommendation model on an Amazon SageMaker real-time endpoint. The team has trained a replacement model and wants to compare the replacement model against the current model by using live request patterns. The replacement model must not return responses to customers until the team confirms that its prediction behavior and latency are acceptable.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Deploy the replacement model to a separate SageMaker endpoint and replay a stored validation dataset to both endpoints.
Replace the current model during an off-peak window and use SageMaker Model Monitor to detect quality changes.
Create a SageMaker shadow test with the current model as the production variant and the replacement model as the shadow variant.
Add the replacement model as a SageMaker production variant with a small traffic weight and increase the weight after review.

correctText: Create a SageMaker shadow test with the current model as the production variant and the replacement model as the shadow variant.
questions.explanationHtml:
SageMaker shadow testing is designed for validating a new model against the model that is already serving production traffic. The production variant continues to handle customer responses, while the shadow variant receives copied inference requests so the team can compare behavior and infrastructure performance without changing the customer-facing result. See the AWS documentation for Overview of SageMaker AI shadow tests and Creation workflow for shadow tests.

This differs from a weighted production variant rollout, where the new model actively serves some portion of live traffic. Weighted variants are appropriate when the team is ready for limited exposure, but the scenario requires observation before any customer response comes from the new model. Shadow tests also provide a practical comparison point for latency, errors, and resource behavior, which can be reviewed in SageMaker and CloudWatch as described in Monitoring shadow tests and SageMaker endpoint CloudWatch metric definitions and dimensions.

questions.promptHtml: A film studio's visual effects ML team runs GPU-based Amazon SageMaker training jobs for multiple movie productions. The team tags the jobs by production and environment. Finance wants to receive notifications when actual month-to-date spend or forecasted monthly spend for a single production approaches an approved limit. The team does not need detailed line-item exports or high-level architectural recommendations. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
questions.promptText:
A film studio's visual effects ML team runs GPU-based Amazon SageMaker training jobs for multiple movie productions. The team tags the jobs by production and environment. Finance wants to receive notifications when actual month-to-date spend or forecasted monthly spend for a single production approaches an approved limit. The team does not need detailed line-item exports or high-level architectural recommendations.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Create an AWS Budgets cost budget filtered by service and an activated production cost allocation tag, and configure actual and forecasted alerts to notify finance.
Enable AWS Cost and Usage Reports delivered to Amazon S3 with production tags, and query the files with Athena after each billing cycle closes.
Use AWS Trusted Advisor Cost Optimization recommendations for the account, and review SageMaker AI Savings Plans purchase recommendations where applicable.
Create an AWS Cost Explorer report filtered by service and production tags, and schedule stakeholders to review the forecast chart each week.

correctText: Create an AWS Budgets cost budget filtered by service and an activated production cost allocation tag, and configure actual and forecasted alerts to notify finance.
questions.explanationHtml:
AWS Budgets is the best fit when the requirement is to define an approved spending threshold and notify stakeholders as actual or forecasted spend approaches that threshold. Budgets can be scoped with filters such as service and activated cost allocation tags, which matches the need to track a single production's SageMaker spending without building a custom reporting pipeline. For more details, see AWS Budgets documentation.

AWS Cost Explorer is better for interactive analysis, custom cost reports, historical trends, and forecasting, but it is primarily an analysis tool rather than the simplest alerting mechanism for a financial threshold. AWS Cost and Usage Reports provide more granular billing data in Amazon S3, but they are better suited for detailed downstream analysis than for simple threshold notifications. AWS Trusted Advisor can identify cost optimization opportunities and other account-level recommendations, including applicable SageMaker AI Savings Plans purchase recommendations, but it does not replace a cost budget for actual and forecasted spend alerts. See AWS Cost Explorer overview, AWS Cost and Usage Reports documentation, and AWS Trusted Advisor Recommendations documentation for the intended roles of these tools.

questions.promptHtml: A legal research publisher's knowledge products team wants to build a prototype that generates concise summaries of long legal memos. The team wants to compare several AWS and third-party pretrained generative models through a managed API, avoid provisioning model hosting infrastructure, and pay based on usage during an unpredictable pilot. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
questions.promptText:
A legal research publisher's knowledge products team wants to build a prototype that generates concise summaries of long legal memos. The team wants to compare several AWS and third-party pretrained generative models through a managed API, avoid provisioning model hosting infrastructure, and pay based on usage during an unpredictable pilot.

Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Use Amazon Bedrock to compare available foundation models, verify required model access permissions, and invoke the selected model through a supported inference API.
Use a SageMaker built-in XGBoost algorithm container to train a summarization model and deploy it to an endpoint.
Use a JumpStart end-to-end solution template for a related use case and customize its generated pipeline resources.
Use SageMaker JumpStart to deploy a selected text generation model to a SageMaker endpoint and invoke the endpoint.

correctText: Use Amazon Bedrock to compare available foundation models, verify required model access permissions, and invoke the selected model through a supported inference API.
questions.explanationHtml:
Amazon Bedrock is the best fit when a team wants managed access to foundation models from AWS and third-party providers without building, training, or hosting the model infrastructure itself. Bedrock exposes model catalog and runtime capabilities so applications can call selected models through supported inference APIs, which aligns well with a pilot that needs fast comparison of generative models and variable usage. In current commercial Regions, access depends on the required account permissions, including AWS Marketplace permissions where applicable, and some providers can have additional first-use requirements. See the Amazon Bedrock documentation on Using models and Model support by feature and Region.

SageMaker JumpStart is also relevant to this skill because it helps users find pretrained models, foundation models, and example notebooks from SageMaker. It is a strong choice when the team wants to start from a model and then manage SageMaker training, fine-tuning, or deployment resources. For the stated requirement, however, a managed model API has less operational overhead than deploying and operating a SageMaker endpoint. The SageMaker documentation describes these capabilities in SageMaker JumpStart.

JumpStart solution templates are documented for Studio Classic, which is no longer available for new onboarding, so they are not the most direct choice for a new prototype that only needs managed generative model invocation. Even where templates are available, they are intended to create example resources and workflows for common ML use cases, which adds customization and lifecycle management compared with calling a foundation model API. For documented JumpStart solution template use cases, see SageMaker JumpStart solutions.

The built-in SageMaker algorithm catalog is important for choosing algorithms by ML problem type, but model selection must match the task. Algorithms such as XGBoost and Linear Learner are excellent for many structured-data problems, while legal memo summarization is a generative text task that is better served by a pretrained generative model. For a broader view of SageMaker built-in algorithms, pretrained models, and templates, see Use Amazon SageMaker built-in algorithms or pre-trained models.

questions.promptHtml: A biotechnology lab trains a PyTorch neural network in Amazon SageMaker to predict molecular activity. The training script publishes validation loss after each epoch. The team currently runs many manual trials across a large hyperparameter space, and many poor trials run to completion. The team wants to improve validation loss while using compute resources more efficiently. Which solution will best meet these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A biotechnology lab trains a PyTorch neural network in Amazon SageMaker to predict molecular activity. The training script publishes validation loss after each epoch. The team currently runs many manual trials across a large hyperparameter space, and many poor trials run to completion. The team wants to improve validation loss while using compute resources more efficiently.

Which solution will best meet these requirements?

options.text: Use SageMaker Automatic Model Tuning with Hyperband, set validation loss as the objective metric, and tune the highest impact hyperparameters.
Use SageMaker Automatic Model Tuning with random search, set validation loss as the objective metric, and maximize parallel training jobs.
Use SageMaker Debugger with custom rules, collect epoch tensors during training, and keep the current hyperparameter search.
Use SageMaker Automatic Model Tuning with grid search, set validation loss as the objective metric, and enumerate all supported hyperparameters.

correctText: Use SageMaker Automatic Model Tuning with Hyperband, set validation loss as the objective metric, and tune the highest impact hyperparameters.
questions.explanationHtml:
SageMaker Automatic Model Tuning improves model development by running multiple training jobs with different hyperparameter values and selecting the model that performs best against a chosen objective metric. In this scenario, validation loss is already emitted after each epoch, which makes the workload suitable for strategies that use intermediate training results.

Hyperband is designed for iterative algorithms, such as many neural network training jobs, because it can use early performance signals to allocate resources more effectively. This is a better fit than brute force grid search or broad random search when the goal is to improve model quality without wasting compute on trials that are unlikely to succeed. AWS also recommends narrowing tuning to the most important hyperparameters because large search spaces make optimization harder and more expensive.

For more information, see Perform automatic model tuning with SageMaker, How hyperparameter tuning works, Best practices for hyperparameter tuning, and Stop training jobs early.

questions.domain: ML Solution Monitoring, Maintenance, and Security
questions.promptHtml: A digital advertising agency's ML governance team uses Amazon SageMaker AI for model training. Data scientists need to start training jobs from SageMaker Studio by using an already approved execution role. That role should read input data from one Amazon S3 prefix and write artifacts to one S3 output prefix. The team must enforce least privilege and prevent users from selecting unapproved roles for jobs. Which actions should the team take? (Select TWO.)
questions.promptText:
A digital advertising agency's ML governance team uses Amazon SageMaker AI for model training. Data scientists need to start training jobs from SageMaker Studio by using an already approved execution role. That role should read input data from one Amazon S3 prefix and write artifacts to one S3 output prefix. The team must enforce least privilege and prevent users from selecting unapproved roles for jobs.

Which actions should the team take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Grant S3 bucket access to each data scientist identity and remove data access permissions from the SageMaker execution role.
Configure the approved SageMaker execution role with SageMaker trust and least-privilege access to the required S3 prefixes and KMS key.
Grant data scientists an IAM identity policy for required SageMaker training actions and iam:PassRole on only the approved execution role.
Grant broad KMS key administrator access to the data scientists and rely on the key policy to constrain SageMaker job creation.
Attach AmazonSageMakerFullAccess and AmazonS3FullAccess to each data scientist, then review CloudTrail for misuse after jobs run.

correctText: Configure the approved SageMaker execution role with SageMaker trust and least-privilege access to the required S3 prefixes and KMS key.
Grant data scientists an IAM identity policy for required SageMaker training actions and iam:PassRole on only the approved execution role.
questions.explanationHtml:
For SageMaker AI training, separate the permissions of the human or application identity from the permissions of the SageMaker execution role. The user or application needs permission to call the required SageMaker APIs, and also needs iam:PassRole for the specific role that SageMaker is allowed to assume. Restricting iam:PassRole to an approved role is the control that prevents users from selecting a different role with broader access.

The execution role is the role that SageMaker assumes while running the job, so it needs a trust relationship for SageMaker and only the permissions required by the workload, such as access to the specific S3 prefixes and applicable KMS key. Attaching broad policies such as full SageMaker and full S3 access is a common anti-pattern because it makes experimentation easy but leaves production access too permissive. CloudTrail can help audit what happened, but it is not a substitute for preventive IAM controls. See the SageMaker IAM overview in Identity and Access Management for Amazon SageMaker AI, execution role guidance in SageMaker AI Roles, and iam:PassRole behavior in Grant a user permissions to pass a role to an AWS service.

questions.promptHtml: A municipal water utility's ML data engineering team receives pump telemetry in Amazon Kinesis Data Streams. The team needs to continuously cleanse records, compute short time-window aggregates, and enrich the stream before writing curated data to Amazon S3 for model training. The existing transformation logic is written in PySpark, and the team wants a managed ETL service with minimal infrastructure administration. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
questions.promptText:
A municipal water utility's ML data engineering team receives pump telemetry in Amazon Kinesis Data Streams. The team needs to continuously cleanse records, compute short time-window aggregates, and enrich the stream before writing curated data to Amazon S3 for model training. The existing transformation logic is written in PySpark, and the team wants a managed ETL service with minimal infrastructure administration.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Configure Amazon Data Firehose to invoke an AWS Lambda function, apply the PySpark transformations, and deliver curated output to Amazon S3.
Build an Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink application that reads from Kinesis Data Streams, rewrites the transformations with Flink APIs, and writes curated output downstream.
Create an AWS Lambda event source mapping for Kinesis Data Streams, run the aggregation logic in Lambda, and write curated batches to Amazon S3.
Create an AWS Glue streaming ETL job that reads from Kinesis Data Streams, applies the PySpark transformations, and writes curated output to Amazon S3.

correctText: Create an AWS Glue streaming ETL job that reads from Kinesis Data Streams, applies the PySpark transformations, and writes curated output to Amazon S3.
questions.explanationHtml:
AWS Glue streaming ETL is the best fit when a team needs continuous data preparation from a streaming source and wants to use Spark-based transformations. Glue streaming jobs use the Spark streaming model, including Spark Structured Streaming micro-batches, so PySpark cleansing, enrichment, and aggregation logic can be used in a managed ETL context. See Adding streaming ETL jobs in AWS Glue and AWS Glue streaming concepts.

Amazon Data Firehose with Lambda is useful when the goal is to buffer, optionally transform, and deliver streaming data to destinations such as Amazon S3. That pattern is best suited to simpler record transformations before delivery, not to preserving a Spark-based ETL workflow with time-window aggregations. See Transform source data in Amazon Data Firehose.

AWS Lambda can consume Kinesis Data Streams records through an event source mapping and can support stateful tumbling-window processing for stream records. For this scenario, the main tradeoff is not whether Lambda can transform or aggregate records, it is whether the service matches the existing PySpark ETL approach with the least operational overhead. See Using AWS Lambda with Amazon Kinesis.

Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink is appropriate for custom Flink streaming applications, especially when teams want to build with Flink APIs for continuous stream processing. It is less suitable here because the team already has PySpark transformations and wants minimal rework. See Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink documentation.

questions.promptHtml: A tax preparation software vendor's ML platform team manages a production Amazon SageMaker model. The team has an existing SageMaker Pipeline that retrains the model. The team needs an auditable record of SageMaker API activity, needs to monitor for a specific write operation that indicates a model promotion, and needs to start the retraining pipeline automatically with minimal custom code. Which solution will meet these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A tax preparation software vendor's ML platform team manages a production Amazon SageMaker model. The team has an existing SageMaker Pipeline that retrains the model. The team needs an auditable record of SageMaker API activity, needs to monitor for a specific write operation that indicates a model promotion, and needs to start the retraining pipeline automatically with minimal custom code.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Configure SageMaker Model Monitor quality checks, create a CloudWatch alarm for drift metrics, and invoke StartPipelineExecution on the retraining pipeline.
Enable CloudTrail data events for the training S3 bucket, query the delivered logs with Athena, and invoke StartPipelineExecution on a schedule.
Configure AWS Config rules for SageMaker endpoint resources, send noncompliance notifications to SNS, and invoke StartPipelineExecution from a subscriber.
Configure a CloudTrail trail for SageMaker management events, create an EventBridge rule for the selected API call, and invoke StartPipelineExecution on the retraining pipeline.

correctText: Configure a CloudTrail trail for SageMaker management events, create an EventBridge rule for the selected API call, and invoke StartPipelineExecution on the retraining pipeline.
questions.explanationHtml:
CloudTrail is the AWS service used for governance, compliance, and auditing of API activity. For SageMaker, CloudTrail records actions taken by users, roles, and AWS services, which makes it the right source when the trigger condition is a management operation such as a model promotion or endpoint-related API call. A trail can also deliver logs to Amazon S3 for longer retention and audit analysis beyond the CloudTrail event history window.

EventBridge is the automation layer that can react to CloudTrail API-call events. An EventBridge rule can match the relevant event pattern and call StartPipelineExecution to start an existing SageMaker Pipeline, which keeps the retraining workflow automated without building a polling system. SageMaker Model Monitor and CloudWatch are better suited to drift and quality thresholds, while AWS Config is better suited to configuration compliance. See AWS CloudTrail overview, Amazon SageMaker AI CloudTrail integration, EventBridge events delivered via CloudTrail, and SageMaker Pipelines with EventBridge.

questions.promptHtml: A specialty pharmacy's ML operations team hosts a medication adherence prediction model on an Amazon SageMaker real-time endpoint. Nurses report intermittent delays during business hours. The team needs to determine whether the delays correlate with endpoint request volume or instance resource pressure. The team must use operational metrics and alarms, not audit logs or model quality reports. Which solution will meet these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A specialty pharmacy's ML operations team hosts a medication adherence prediction model on an Amazon SageMaker real-time endpoint. Nurses report intermittent delays during business hours. The team needs to determine whether the delays correlate with endpoint request volume or instance resource pressure. The team must use operational metrics and alarms, not audit logs or model quality reports.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Create an AWS CloudTrail trail that delivers SageMaker API activity logs to Amazon S3 for later analysis.
Create a SageMaker Model Monitor schedule to detect data quality drift and publish violation reports to Amazon S3.
Create Amazon CloudWatch dashboards and alarms for SageMaker endpoint invocations, latency, and instance utilization metrics.
Create AWS Config rules to evaluate SageMaker endpoint configuration changes and send noncompliance notifications.

correctText: Create Amazon CloudWatch dashboards and alarms for SageMaker endpoint invocations, latency, and instance utilization metrics.
questions.explanationHtml:
Amazon CloudWatch is the primary service for operational monitoring of SageMaker infrastructure. For a real-time endpoint, the mental model is that the endpoint is a production service with traffic, latency, errors, and host-level resource pressure that must be observed over time. CloudWatch dashboards and alarms let an ML operations team correlate business-hour delays with metrics such as invocations, latency, and utilization, then notify operators or drive follow-up actions.

SageMaker Model Monitor addresses a different class of problem: whether production data and model behavior are drifting from expected baselines. CloudTrail answers audit questions such as who made an API call, while AWS Config answers configuration and compliance questions such as how a resource changed over time. Those services are valuable in an ML operations environment, but they do not replace CloudWatch for endpoint performance monitoring. For more information, see Monitor Amazon SageMaker with Amazon CloudWatch and Monitor workload resources.

questions.promptHtml: An online grocery retailer's demand forecasting team uses a Git repository for training and inference code. The team now needs a release process that separates build automation from deployment orchestration, runs validation before any endpoint update, and prevents production changes until a reviewer approves the candidate model.
