questions.promptHtml: A digital publishing group's ML platform team tags Amazon SageMaker training jobs, notebooks, and endpoints by Project. The team must keep a new recommendation model pilot within a monthly spend target. The finance team wants an alert before the pilot is likely to exceed the target, and the platform team wants the alert delivered to an existing SNS topic used for ML cost notifications. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
questions.promptText:
A digital publishing group's ML platform team tags Amazon SageMaker training jobs, notebooks, and endpoints by Project. The team must keep a new recommendation model pilot within a monthly spend target. The finance team wants an alert before the pilot is likely to exceed the target, and the platform team wants the alert delivered to an existing SNS topic used for ML cost notifications.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Create an Amazon QuickSight dashboard for the Project tag. Visualize pilot spend trends and share the dashboard with the platform team.
Create an AWS Budgets cost budget filtered by the Project tag. Configure a forecasted threshold notification that publishes to the SNS topic.
Create an AWS Cost Explorer report filtered by the Project tag. Review the forecast weekly and manually publish updates to the SNS topic.
Enable AWS Trusted Advisor cost optimization checks for the account. Review underutilized resources and manually notify the SNS topic.

correctText: Create an AWS Budgets cost budget filtered by the Project tag. Configure a forecasted threshold notification that publishes to the SNS topic.
questions.explanationHtml:
AWS Budgets is the best fit when the requirement is to define a spend target and receive threshold notifications. Budgets supports cost, usage, reservation, and Savings Plans budget types, and budgets can be filtered by dimensions such as service, linked account, Region, and tags. For ML workloads, tagging resources by project or activity is a practical way to track spend for training, hosting, notebooks, and experiments separately.

A forecasted threshold notification helps the team react before the pilot is expected to exceed its monthly target. Sending the notification through Amazon SNS fits an operational notification pattern because the alert can reach the existing cost notification workflow without building custom polling or reporting logic.

AWS Cost Explorer and AWS Trusted Advisor are still valuable cost tools, but they solve different problems. Cost Explorer helps teams analyze cost and usage trends, create reports, and view forecasts, while Trusted Advisor cost optimization checks help find underutilized or idle resources and savings opportunities. Neither is the lowest overhead way to create a tag-filtered monthly budget with forecasted threshold notifications.

For more information, see AWS Budgets overview, AWS Cost Explorer overview, and Trusted Advisor cost optimization checks.

questions.promptHtml: A public transit authority's ridership analytics team trains a deep learning model in Amazon SageMaker to predict station crowding levels. The team notices that the saved model artifact is becoming larger after each architecture change, and the endpoint now requires more memory than planned. The team wants to reduce the model footprint while keeping the same training dataset and deployment workflow. Which action will MOST directly address the model footprint?
questions.promptText:
A public transit authority's ridership analytics team trains a deep learning model in Amazon SageMaker to predict station crowding levels. The team notices that the saved model artifact is becoming larger after each architecture change, and the endpoint now requires more memory than planned. The team wants to reduce the model footprint while keeping the same training dataset and deployment workflow.

Which action will MOST directly address the model footprint?

options.text: Simplify the network topology by reducing hidden layers and units, then validate the accuracy tradeoff.
Move the training data to a different S3 storage class, then rerun the existing training job.
Enable SageMaker distributed data parallel training, then split the dataset across more GPU instances.
Increase the number of parallel tuning jobs, then select the trial with the lowest validation loss.

correctText: Simplify the network topology by reducing hidden layers and units, then validate the accuracy tradeoff.
questions.explanationHtml:
For a deep learning model, the main mental model is that model size follows parameter count. Layers, hidden units, embeddings, and other trainable structures create weights that must be saved as model artifacts and loaded for inference. AWS describes SageMaker model artifacts as trained parameters, model definition, and metadata, commonly stored after training, in ModelArtifacts.

The most direct way to reduce the footprint is to make the architecture smaller, for example by reducing depth or width, and then testing whether the resulting accuracy is still acceptable. This is a practical accuracy versus complexity tradeoff: a smaller model can be cheaper and easier to host, but it may lose predictive power if simplified too aggressively.

Distributed training and hyperparameter tuning are useful model development tools, but they solve different problems. Data parallelism can help train faster on large datasets, while tuning can search for better settings. Neither guarantees a smaller artifact unless the search space or architecture is explicitly constrained to smaller models. The SageMaker model parallelism documentation discusses how model memory footprint scales with parameter count in Model Parallelism.

questions.promptHtml: A semiconductor fabrication lab's quality engineering team is training a convolutional neural network in Amazon SageMaker to classify microscopic wafer defect images. The team has a limited labeled dataset and is using SageMaker Automatic Model Tuning to run training jobs. The training code emits validation accuracy after each epoch. The latest training run shows steadily improving training accuracy, but validation accuracy peaks early and then declines as training continues. The team wants to improve the model's ability to generalize to new wafer images without collecting more labeled data. Which TWO actions should the team take? (Select TWO.)
questions.promptText:
A semiconductor fabrication lab's quality engineering team is training a convolutional neural network in Amazon SageMaker to classify microscopic wafer defect images. The team has a limited labeled dataset and is using SageMaker Automatic Model Tuning to run training jobs. The training code emits validation accuracy after each epoch. The latest training run shows steadily improving training accuracy, but validation accuracy peaks early and then declines as training continues. The team wants to improve the model's ability to generalize to new wafer images without collecting more labeled data.

Which TWO actions should the team take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Enable early stopping for the SageMaker hyperparameter tuning job.
Increase regularization in the neural network training configuration.
Increase the number of training epochs for every tuning trial.
Add more convolutional layers to increase model capacity.
Select the model version with the highest training accuracy.

correctText: Enable early stopping for the SageMaker hyperparameter tuning job.
Increase regularization in the neural network training configuration.
questions.explanationHtml:
The important signal is the divergence between training accuracy and validation accuracy. When training accuracy continues to improve but validation accuracy peaks and then worsens, the model is likely learning details of the training set that do not generalize. SageMaker guidance on training and validation curves describes using these curves to identify this pattern and considering corrective actions such as more regularization: Amazon SageMaker training and validation curves.

Early stopping is a practical control because it stops unpromising or non-improving training jobs before they continue consuming compute and fitting noise. In SageMaker Automatic Model Tuning, early stopping can stop training jobs that are not improving the objective metric, which is especially useful when iterative algorithms emit metrics during training: Use early stopping for tuning jobs.

Regularization changes the training objective or training process so the model is less free to memorize the training data. Depending on the algorithm and framework, this can include dropout, L1 regularization, L2 regularization, or weight decay. For SageMaker built-in algorithms, examples include Linear Learner parameters such as l1 and wd, and XGBoost parameters such as alpha, lambda, eta, gamma, and max_depth: Linear Learner hyperparameters and XGBoost hyperparameters.

Adding more epochs, adding model layers, or choosing the model with the highest training accuracy all push in the wrong direction for this scenario. Those actions either increase the opportunity to memorize a limited dataset or ignore the validation evidence that the model is already overfitting.

questions.promptHtml: A warehouse robotics manufacturer's data engineering team ingests telemetry from autonomous forklifts into Amazon MSK. Firmware teams change telemetry fields over time. Downstream Apache Spark and Managed Service for Apache Flink jobs need an efficient binary interchange format that preserves schema information so the data can be processed later without depending on the source system's context. Which action should the team take?
questions.promptText:
A warehouse robotics manufacturer's data engineering team ingests telemetry from autonomous forklifts into Amazon MSK. Firmware teams change telemetry fields over time. Downstream Apache Spark and Managed Service for Apache Flink jobs need an efficient binary interchange format that preserves schema information so the data can be processed later without depending on the source system's context.

Which action should the team take?

options.text: Serialize the telemetry events as CSV before publishing them to the stream.
Serialize the telemetry events as Apache Parquet before publishing them to the stream.
Serialize the telemetry events as Apache Avro before publishing them to the stream.
Serialize the telemetry events as JSON before publishing them to the stream.

correctText: Serialize the telemetry events as Apache Avro before publishing them to the stream.
questions.explanationHtml:
Apache Avro is designed for efficient serialization and data interchange in big data systems. It is commonly used with streaming and distributed processing technologies because it can keep schema information close to the data, which helps consumers interpret records even as producers evolve the structure over time.

Parquet and ORC are better mental models for analytics storage, especially when query engines read only selected columns from large datasets. JSON and CSV are easier for humans to inspect, but that readability comes with tradeoffs in compactness, schema handling, and validation. For streaming telemetry with changing fields, the key requirement is not human readability or column pruning, it is schema-aware binary interchange.

AWS services can work with several of these formats depending on the stage of the ML data pipeline. For example, AWS Glue documents format handling for Spark ETL jobs in Data format options for inputs and outputs in AWS Glue for Spark, and schema validation concepts for streaming applications in AWS Glue Schema Registry. The practical decision is to match the format to the access pattern: Avro for evolving stream records, Parquet or ORC for columnar analytics, and CSV or JSON for simpler interchange or inspection.

questions.promptHtml: A municipal housing agency's analytics team trains a tabular model in Amazon SageMaker to prioritize building inspections. After reviewing sample predictions, the team is concerned that a numeric property attribute might be acting as an indirect proxy for neighborhood conditions. The team needs a repeatable way to understand how much each input column contributed to the model's predictions for the scored records. Which action should the ML engineer take?
questions.promptText:
A municipal housing agency's analytics team trains a tabular model in Amazon SageMaker to prioritize building inspections. After reviewing sample predictions, the team is concerned that a numeric property attribute might be acting as an indirect proxy for neighborhood conditions. The team needs a repeatable way to understand how much each input column contributed to the model's predictions for the scored records.

Which action should the ML engineer take?

options.text: Query CloudWatch Logs Insights for prediction request fields and aggregate counts.
Run a SageMaker Clarify explainability analysis to generate SHAP feature attribution values.
Create a SageMaker Model Monitor data quality baseline from the training dataset.
Use QuickSight ML insights to detect anomalies in the scored prediction dataset.

correctText: Run a SageMaker Clarify explainability analysis to generate SHAP feature attribution values.
questions.explanationHtml:
SageMaker Clarify is the AWS service feature designed for model bias analysis and explainability in SageMaker workflows. For explaining predictions, Clarify uses SHAP feature attributions, which are based on Shapley values from game theory and estimate how much each feature contributed to a prediction. This is useful when an apparently ordinary input column might be carrying unintended signal, because the team can inspect feature influence instead of relying only on aggregate model metrics.

Model Monitor data quality baselines are useful for detecting drift in feature statistics over time, but they do not answer why a prediction was made. CloudWatch Logs Insights can analyze operational logs, and QuickSight can help visualize or detect anomalies in business data, but neither computes model explanation metrics. For this requirement, the right mental model is that model performance metrics such as accuracy or F1 tell you how well the model performed, while explainability metrics such as SHAP attributions help reveal what drove the model behavior. For more information, see SageMaker Clarify Shapley Values and SageMaker Clarify Model Explainability.

questions.promptHtml: An airline maintenance analytics team is evaluating several Amazon SageMaker Autopilot candidate models that predict the number of flight hours remaining before an aircraft component requires replacement. The target variable is continuous. Operations leaders want a validation metric that is easy to interpret in flight-hour units and that penalizes occasional large prediction errors more heavily than small prediction errors. Which action should the ML engineer take to analyze model performance?
questions.promptText:
An airline maintenance analytics team is evaluating several Amazon SageMaker Autopilot candidate models that predict the number of flight hours remaining before an aircraft component requires replacement. The target variable is continuous. Operations leaders want a validation metric that is easy to interpret in flight-hour units and that penalizes occasional large prediction errors more heavily than small prediction errors.

Which action should the ML engineer take to analyze model performance?

options.text: Compare candidate models by using R2 on a held-out validation set.
Compare candidate models by using F1 on a held-out validation set.
Compare candidate models by using MAE on a held-out validation set.
Compare candidate models by using RMSE on a held-out validation set.

correctText: Compare candidate models by using RMSE on a held-out validation set.
questions.explanationHtml:
For a regression problem, the model predicts a continuous value rather than a class label. Metrics such as RMSE, MAE, and R2 are common choices, but they answer different operational questions.

RMSE is the best fit when large errors should matter more than small errors. It squares each error before averaging, which increases the influence of outliers or severe misses, and then takes the square root so the result is expressed in the same unit as the target, such as flight hours. This makes it useful when a maintenance team needs an error measure that is both interpretable and sensitive to high-impact mistakes.

MAE is often easier to explain because it is the average absolute error in the original unit, but it does not amplify larger misses. R2 is useful for understanding explained variance, but it is unitless and does not directly describe the size of prediction errors. F1, precision, recall, AUC, and confusion matrices are primarily classification-oriented metrics, so they are not the right way to compare models that predict a continuous numeric value.

Amazon SageMaker Autopilot reports model validation metrics by problem type, including regression metrics such as RMSE, MAE, MSE, and R2, as described in SageMaker Autopilot model validation metrics. Autopilot model quality reports can also help interpret model performance for classification use cases, including confusion matrices and threshold tradeoffs, as described in SageMaker Autopilot model insights.

questions.promptHtml: An online grocery marketplace's pricing ML team uses tabular features such as item demand velocity, store-level stockout counts, promotion status, and local weather summaries. A streaming workflow updates the latest demand and stockout signals throughout the day for a substitution-ranking endpoint. A nightly Spark workflow creates historical aggregates from data in Amazon S3 for retraining. Data scientists on several product teams need to discover approved feature definitions and build training datasets from past feature values, while the serving application needs the current feature records at request time. Which actions should the team take? (Select TWO.)
questions.promptText:
An online grocery marketplace's pricing ML team uses tabular features such as item demand velocity, store-level stockout counts, promotion status, and local weather summaries. A streaming workflow updates the latest demand and stockout signals throughout the day for a substitution-ranking endpoint. A nightly Spark workflow creates historical aggregates from data in Amazon S3 for retraining. Data scientists on several product teams need to discover approved feature definitions and build training datasets from past feature values, while the serving application needs the current feature records at request time.

Which actions should the team take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Configure the feature groups with online and offline stores for serving and training access patterns.
Register each trained model in Amazon SageMaker Model Registry and store feature values as model metadata.
Store transformed feature files only in Amazon S3 and have endpoints read those files for each prediction.
Export separate SageMaker Data Wrangler notebooks for each team to run before training and inference.
Create Amazon SageMaker Feature Store feature groups for the curated ML features.

correctText: Configure the feature groups with online and offline stores for serving and training access patterns.
Create Amazon SageMaker Feature Store feature groups for the curated ML features.
questions.explanationHtml:
Amazon SageMaker Feature Store is designed to help teams create, store, share, and retrieve ML features for training and inference workflows. A feature group gives the team a managed container for related feature definitions and records, which helps make curated features easier to discover and reuse across product teams. See the AWS documentation for Amazon SageMaker Feature Store.

The important design choice in this scenario is that the team has two different access patterns. The online store supports request-time access to current feature records, while the offline store supports historical and batch access patterns, such as building training datasets from past feature values. Using both stores lets the team support serving and retraining workflows from the same managed feature organization. See Feature Store storage configurations and Ingest data into Feature Store.

SageMaker Data Wrangler can still be useful for preparing, transforming, and featurizing data, but exporting separate notebooks for each team does not by itself provide managed feature discovery or serving. SageMaker Model Registry manages model versions and approvals, not feature serving. Storing files only in Amazon S3 can support batch training workflows, especially for analytics, but it does not provide the online feature access required by a real-time endpoint. See Amazon SageMaker Data Wrangler.

questions.promptHtml: A nonprofit microlending consortium's analytics team is preparing tabular training data for a loan approval model. The team suspects that applicants from one community are underrepresented and that historical positive approval labels differ across communities. The team must assess the dataset before training and use a managed, low-code SageMaker workflow to reduce representation imbalance when the assessment confirms it. Which solution best meets these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A nonprofit microlending consortium's analytics team is preparing tabular training data for a loan approval model. The team suspects that applicants from one community are underrepresented and that historical positive approval labels differ across communities. The team must assess the dataset before training and use a managed, low-code SageMaker workflow to reduce representation imbalance when the assessment confirms it.

Which solution best meets these requirements?

options.text: Deploy the model with SageMaker Model Monitor, then create a data quality baseline from live endpoint traffic.
Generate a SageMaker Clarify pre-training bias report in Data Wrangler, then apply a Data Wrangler balance data transform.
Run SageMaker Experiments trials with multiple algorithms, then choose the trial with the highest overall validation F1 score.
Catalog the training data with an AWS Glue crawler, then remove the community attribute from the training dataset.

correctText: Generate a SageMaker Clarify pre-training bias report in Data Wrangler, then apply a Data Wrangler balance data transform.
questions.explanationHtml:
SageMaker Clarify is the best fit when an ML team needs to measure potential bias in a dataset before model training. Pre-training bias analysis focuses on the training data itself, such as whether one facet is underrepresented or whether label outcomes differ between facet values. The team can generate these reports during data preparation, including from SageMaker Studio and Data Wrangler, as described in Overview of pre-training data bias in Amazon SageMaker Clarify and Generate pre-training bias reports in SageMaker Studio.

After the team identifies representation imbalance, Data Wrangler is a practical low-code place to apply dataset transformations before training. Its balancing operations can help reduce underrepresentation in the prepared training data, although the engineer should still validate whether the transformed data improves fairness and model performance. The relevant transformation category is documented in Transform data in Data Wrangler.

Model Monitor is valuable later in the lifecycle, especially after a model is deployed and a baseline exists, but it does not satisfy a requirement to assess raw training data before training. SageMaker Experiments is useful for comparing model runs, but an aggregate metric can mask subgroup problems. Removing the community attribute without measurement is also insufficient because bias can remain through proxy variables such as geography, income, or employment patterns.

questions.domain: Deployment and Orchestration of ML Workflows
questions.promptHtml: A regional grocery chain's demand forecasting team runs weekly batch forecasts for store inventory planning. Confirmed sales labels are finalized at the end of each month. The team wants to retrain the forecasting model on a fixed monthly schedule, run preprocessing and evaluation consistently, and make the new model available as a candidate that requires approval before it can be deployed. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST custom workflow code?
questions.promptText:
A regional grocery chain's demand forecasting team runs weekly batch forecasts for store inventory planning. Confirmed sales labels are finalized at the end of each month. The team wants to retrain the forecasting model on a fixed monthly schedule, run preprocessing and evaluation consistently, and make the new model available as a candidate that requires approval before it can be deployed.

Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST custom workflow code?

options.text: Use SageMaker Batch Transform monthly on the labeled data, then copy the batch output to the production model artifact location.
Use SageMaker Experiments to create a monthly trial, then have analysts manually run preprocessing and training notebooks.
Use EventBridge to start a SageMaker Pipeline that processes labeled data, trains, evaluates, and registers the model in Model Registry.
Use an AWS CodeBuild project on a monthly schedule to run scripts that preprocess, train, evaluate, and update production.

correctText: Use EventBridge to start a SageMaker Pipeline that processes labeled data, trains, evaluates, and registers the model in Model Registry.
questions.explanationHtml:
A scheduled retraining workflow is a good fit for Amazon EventBridge plus SageMaker Pipelines. EventBridge supplies the time-based trigger, while the pipeline defines repeatable steps for preprocessing, training, evaluation, and any conditional logic needed to decide whether a newly trained model should become a candidate. See Scheduling or event-triggering SageMaker Pipeline runs with Amazon EventBridge and SageMaker Pipelines step types.

The approval requirement is handled by SageMaker Model Registry. Instead of immediately replacing a production model, the retraining workflow can register a new versioned model package with evaluation metadata so reviewers can approve or reject it before deployment. This creates traceability and governance without requiring a team to build a custom registry or manual file-copy process. See SageMaker Model Registry concepts for model groups and versioned model packages.

Batch Transform is useful when the team needs predictions for a dataset, but it does not train a new model. SageMaker Experiments helps track and compare ML work, but relying on analysts to run notebooks does not minimize custom workflow effort. CodeBuild is a general build service, so using it as the main ML orchestrator would require more custom scripting than using managed SageMaker workflow components.

questions.promptHtml: A national museum's digitization team is classifying scanned artifact images into known catalog categories. The team has a few hundred labeled images for each category, no requirement to locate objects within the image, and limited budget for experimentation. The team wants to minimize training cost and development effort while still using an ML-based approach. Which TWO model-selection actions should the team take?
questions.promptText:
A national museum's digitization team is classifying scanned artifact images into known catalog categories. The team has a few hundred labeled images for each category, no requirement to locate objects within the image, and limited budget for experimentation. The team wants to minimize training cost and development effort while still using an ML-based approach.

Which TWO model-selection actions should the team take?

options.text: Train a SageMaker built-in image classification model in transfer learning mode from pretrained weights.
Evaluate Amazon Rekognition Custom Labels with the labeled images before building a custom vision model.
Train a SageMaker object detection model to predict bounding boxes and category labels for every artifact.
Train a SageMaker built-in image classification model in full training mode with random initial weights.
Implement a custom deep CNN container and tune many architecture hyperparameters with grid search.

correctText: Train a SageMaker built-in image classification model in transfer learning mode from pretrained weights.
Evaluate Amazon Rekognition Custom Labels with the labeled images before building a custom vision model.
questions.explanationHtml:
When cost is a key constraint, model selection should start with the least complex approach that can meet the requirement. For a known image classification task with limited labeled data, a managed computer vision service or a pretrained image classification model with transfer learning can reduce both training time and engineering effort.

Transfer learning is especially cost-effective because pretrained convolutional layers already encode general visual features, so training can focus on adapting the final classification behavior to the museum's categories. By contrast, full training from random weights, object detection, and custom CNN architecture search all increase the amount of data, tuning, labeling, or infrastructure needed. SageMaker documentation describes the tradeoffs among pretrained models, built-in algorithms, framework code, and custom containers in Choose an algorithm, and maps common use cases to built-in algorithms and pretrained models in Use Amazon SageMaker built-in algorithms or pretrained models.

questions.domain: ML Solution Monitoring, Maintenance, and Security
questions.promptHtml: A pharmaceutical clinical trials analytics team runs Amazon SageMaker training jobs on patient outcome data in Amazon S3. The S3 objects were recently changed from SSE-S3 encryption to SSE-KMS encryption with a customer managed AWS KMS key. Since the change, the training job fails with an AccessDenied error when reading the training objects. The SageMaker execution role and the S3 bucket policy already allow the required S3 access. Security requirements state that KMS encryption must remain enabled and permissions must follow least privilege. Which action should the ML engineer take to resolve the issue?
questions.promptText:
A pharmaceutical clinical trials analytics team runs Amazon SageMaker training jobs on patient outcome data in Amazon S3. The S3 objects were recently changed from SSE-S3 encryption to SSE-KMS encryption with a customer managed AWS KMS key. Since the change, the training job fails with an AccessDenied error when reading the training objects. The SageMaker execution role and the S3 bucket policy already allow the required S3 access. Security requirements state that KMS encryption must remain enabled and permissions must follow least privilege.

Which action should the ML engineer take to resolve the issue?

options.text: Add the SageMaker training job execution role to the custom KMS key policy for the key.
Remove SSE-KMS from the S3 bucket and store the training objects with SSE-S3.
Attach AmazonSageMakerFullAccess to the user who starts the SageMaker training job.
Enable inter-container traffic encryption on the SageMaker training job configuration.

correctText: Add the SageMaker training job execution role to the custom KMS key policy for the key.
questions.explanationHtml:
When Amazon S3 objects are encrypted with SSE-KMS, successful access requires more than permission to call S3 APIs. The role that reads the objects must also be authorized to use the relevant AWS KMS key. In a SageMaker training job, that role is typically the SageMaker execution role, not necessarily the IAM user who submitted the job.

A customer managed KMS key is controlled by its key policy, together with IAM policies and other policy layers. If the S3 permissions already allow access but the failure begins after switching to a customer managed key, the correct troubleshooting path is to check whether the execution role is allowed by the key policy to use that key. This preserves least privilege because it fixes the missing authorization at the key layer instead of granting broad SageMaker permissions or weakening encryption.

Inter-container traffic encryption is a separate SageMaker security control for protecting communication between containers during training. It is useful for sensitive distributed training workloads, but it does not affect whether a role can use a KMS key. For more detail, see AWS KMS policy evaluation, SageMaker AI IAM troubleshooting, and Troubleshoot access denied errors in IAM.

questions.promptHtml: A mobile game studio's player analytics team is preparing tabular training data in Amazon S3 for a churn prediction model. The data includes categorical fields such as platform and region, numeric activity fields with highly skewed distributions, and hundreds of raw event counters. The team wants to create a better training set and quickly understand whether feature choices improve model performance before running full training jobs. Which TWO actions should the team take?
questions.promptText:
A mobile game studio's player analytics team is preparing tabular training data in Amazon S3 for a churn prediction model. The data includes categorical fields such as platform and region, numeric activity fields with highly skewed distributions, and hundreds of raw event counters. The team wants to create a better training set and quickly understand whether feature choices improve model performance before running full training jobs.

Which TWO actions should the team take?

options.text: Build a SageMaker Data Wrangler flow and use Quick Model to compare candidate feature sets.
Apply logarithmic scaling to skewed numeric activity fields and one-hot encode categorical platform fields.
Use Amazon QuickSight forecasting to generate transformed labels before training the churn model.
Use KNN imputation to average missing platform values across nearest numerical records.
Retain all raw event counters and rely on model training to ignore unhelpful dimensions.

correctText: Build a SageMaker Data Wrangler flow and use Quick Model to compare candidate feature sets.
Apply logarithmic scaling to skewed numeric activity fields and one-hot encode categorical platform fields.
questions.explanationHtml:
Feature engineering is the process of selecting, transforming, and creating features so that the model receives useful signal instead of raw noise. In this scenario, skewed numerical activity fields can benefit from transformations such as a logarithmic transform, and categorical fields such as platform or region usually need encoding before many ML algorithms can use them effectively.

SageMaker Data Wrangler is a good fit when a team needs to import data, visualize distributions, apply built-in or custom transformations, and iterate quickly on preprocessing choices. Its Quick Model capability is useful for checking whether a set of transformations appears promising before the team spends time and money on a full training and tuning workflow. See Overview of Amazon SageMaker Data Wrangler and Transform data.

The distractors fail because they either avoid feature engineering, use a method that does not match the data type, or choose a service intended for analysis rather than ML feature preparation. A model is not guaranteed to ignore irrelevant dimensions efficiently, and adding every raw counter can make the learning problem larger and sparser. For productionized preprocessing after the team settles on transformations, SageMaker Processing jobs are commonly used to run preprocessing and feature engineering workloads on managed infrastructure, as described in Use processing jobs to run data transformation workloads.

questions.domain: Deployment and Orchestration of ML Workflows
questions.promptHtml: A renewable energy operator's forecasting team trains an Amazon SageMaker model that estimates next-day power output for thousands of wind turbines. Each evening, the team writes a complete inference dataset to Amazon S3. The business can wait until the next morning for results, and the team does not need an endpoint that accepts individual prediction requests during the day. The team wants to minimize idle compute cost and avoid managing endpoint capacity. Which deployment strategy should the team choose?
questions.promptText:
A renewable energy operator's forecasting team trains an Amazon SageMaker model that estimates next-day power output for thousands of wind turbines. Each evening, the team writes a complete inference dataset to Amazon S3. The business can wait until the next morning for results, and the team does not need an endpoint that accepts individual prediction requests during the day. The team wants to minimize idle compute cost and avoid managing endpoint capacity.

Which deployment strategy should the team choose?

options.text: Deploy an Amazon SageMaker real-time endpoint for per-turbine requests.
Deploy an Amazon SageMaker serverless endpoint for the nightly file.
Run an Amazon SageMaker batch transform job on the nightly dataset.
Deploy an Amazon SageMaker asynchronous endpoint for queued predictions.

correctText: Run an Amazon SageMaker batch transform job on the nightly dataset.
questions.explanationHtml:
For SageMaker deployment choices, start by asking whether the application needs an endpoint that is available for individual requests. Batch transform is the natural fit when the input is an offline dataset, the results can be produced later, and there is no need to keep model hosting infrastructure available between jobs.

Real-time inference is intended for interactive workloads with low-latency requirements. Serverless inference is useful when you still need endpoint-style invocation but want less infrastructure management and can tolerate cold starts. Asynchronous inference is for queued request processing, especially when individual requests have large payloads or long processing times but still need near-real-time behavior.

The important tradeoff is cost versus responsiveness. If the business process is naturally file-based and can wait for an offline job to complete, a persistent or request-oriented endpoint adds complexity without adding value. See the SageMaker deployment overview in Deploy models for inference and the batch transform guidance in Use Batch Transform.

questions.domain: Deployment and Orchestration of ML Workflows
questions.promptHtml: A sports media streaming platform's ML operations team maintains feature engineering scripts, training code, and endpoint deployment templates for an Amazon SageMaker model. Several engineers change these files each week. The team wants a workflow that preserves change history, supports isolated work before integration, and provides a reliable source for an automated CI/CD pipeline. Which solution best meets these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A sports media streaming platform's ML operations team maintains feature engineering scripts, training code, and endpoint deployment templates for an Amazon SageMaker model. Several engineers change these files each week. The team wants a workflow that preserves change history, supports isolated work before integration, and provides a reliable source for an automated CI/CD pipeline.

Which solution best meets these requirements?

options.text: Store each script revision in versioned S3 prefixes, update a latest prefix manually, and point the pipeline to that prefix.
Use a Git repository, create feature branches, commit changes locally, and push reviewed merges for the pipeline to consume.
Build a new Amazon ECR image after every edit, tag images by engineer name, and deploy the newest image tag.
Register each trained model in SageMaker Model Registry, store source repository details as model metadata, and deploy approved model packages.

correctText: Use a Git repository, create feature branches, commit changes locally, and push reviewed merges for the pipeline to consume.
questions.explanationHtml:
A Git repository is the right control point for scripts, notebooks, infrastructure templates, and other project code because it records changes as commits and supports isolated work through branches. A typical workflow is to clone or pull the repository, make changes, stage and commit those changes, push them to the shared repository, and merge through the team's review process.

In an ML operations setting, that repository becomes the source of truth that an automated build or deployment pipeline can consume. SageMaker Projects are designed around this idea, using code repositories and pipelines to organize ML lifecycle activities such as building images, preparing data, training models, deploying models, and monitoring updates.

Amazon S3, SageMaker Model Registry, and Amazon ECR are important parts of ML systems, but they serve different purposes. S3 stores data and artifacts, Model Registry manages model package versions and approvals, and ECR stores container images. None of these replaces the branch, commit, merge, and review workflow that Git provides for source code.

For more information, see What is AWS CodeCommit?, Basic Git commands, and Automate MLOps with SageMaker Projects.

questions.promptHtml: A maritime logistics firm's route optimization team retrains an Amazon SageMaker model after each quarterly shipment data refresh. The team must retain a repeatable record of every production candidate, including the model artifact location, evaluation metrics, descriptive metadata, and the approval decision before promotion. The team wants to reduce custom tracking code and make audits easier. Which solution will best meet these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A maritime logistics firm's route optimization team retrains an Amazon SageMaker model after each quarterly shipment data refresh. The team must retain a repeatable record of every production candidate, including the model artifact location, evaluation metrics, descriptive metadata, and the approval decision before promotion. The team wants to reduce custom tracking code and make audits easier.

Which solution will best meet these requirements?

options.text: Track each training run in SageMaker Experiments, compare trial metrics, and deploy the trial with the best validation score.
Register each candidate in SageMaker Model Registry, attach metrics and metadata, and use approval status before deployment.
Query training and deployment logs with CloudWatch Logs Insights, save the queries, and rebuild release history during audits.
Store each candidate artifact in Amazon S3, enable bucket versioning, and deploy the latest object prefix after validation.

correctText: Register each candidate in SageMaker Model Registry, attach metrics and metadata, and use approval status before deployment.
questions.explanationHtml:
SageMaker Model Registry is the right fit when a team needs repeatability, production model version management, and audit-friendly release records. It provides a catalog for model versions, lets teams associate metadata and evaluation information with candidates, and supports approval status as part of a controlled promotion process. See the SageMaker Model Registry overview and Model Registry model version documentation.

S3 object versioning is useful for preserving files, and SageMaker Experiments is useful for comparing development runs, but neither is a replacement for a registry that manages production model versions and approval workflow. CloudWatch Logs Insights can help investigate operational events, but using logs as the primary system of record is an anti-pattern for auditability because the team must reconstruct relationships after the fact. For broader reproducibility across datasets, jobs, artifacts, models, and endpoints, SageMaker lineage features can complement Model Registry, as described in SageMaker ML Lineage Tracking.

questions.promptHtml: A metropolitan transit authority's ridership forecasting team prepares engineered features from fare taps, vehicle telemetry, and weather data. Historical training pipelines need batch access to curated feature values, and a deployed Amazon SageMaker endpoint needs low-latency access to the same approved feature definitions during inference. The team currently copies feature calculation logic into multiple notebooks and services, which has caused inconsistent training and inference behavior. The team wants to reduce duplicate feature logic and improve feature reuse. Which solution will meet these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A metropolitan transit authority's ridership forecasting team prepares engineered features from fare taps, vehicle telemetry, and weather data. Historical training pipelines need batch access to curated feature values, and a deployed Amazon SageMaker endpoint needs low-latency access to the same approved feature definitions during inference. The team currently copies feature calculation logic into multiple notebooks and services, which has caused inconsistent training and inference behavior. The team wants to reduce duplicate feature logic and improve feature reuse.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Export a SageMaker Data Wrangler flow to notebooks, and copy the generated transformation code into each training and inference application.
Query the raw source data with Amazon Athena, and call the same SQL queries from training jobs and endpoints.
Register the trained models in SageMaker Model Registry, and attach the feature calculation rules as model package metadata.
Publish the curated features to Amazon SageMaker Feature Store, and use the offline store for training and the online store for inference.

correctText: Publish the curated features to Amazon SageMaker Feature Store, and use the offline store for training and the online store for inference.
questions.explanationHtml:
Amazon SageMaker Feature Store is the best fit when the same engineered features must be reused across training and inference. It provides a managed repository for curated feature records, with an offline store for historical and batch use cases and an online store for low-latency retrieval during inference. This helps reduce training-serving skew, which commonly happens when teams copy feature logic into separate notebooks, pipelines, and applications.

SageMaker Data Wrangler is valuable earlier in the preparation workflow because it helps import, analyze, transform, and featurize data. However, Data Wrangler is not the shared serving system for feature values, so exporting flows and copying code into several consumers does not address feature reuse or consistency. SageMaker Model Registry solves a different MLOps problem, model version governance, while Athena is better suited to SQL analysis over data in Amazon S3 than to per-request feature retrieval by an endpoint.

The practical pattern is to prepare and validate features with tools such as Data Wrangler, Spark, or other processing jobs, then publish approved feature values into Feature Store. This adds an ingestion and management step, but the tradeoff is better consistency, discoverability, and reuse across multiple ML workflows. For more information, see Amazon SageMaker Feature Store and SageMaker Data Wrangler overview.

questions.promptHtml: An industrial robotics manufacturer's telemetry team ingests high-frequency device events for an ML feature pipeline. Producers write to an Amazon Kinesis Data Streams stream in provisioned mode, and a Spark-based consumer writes transformed features to Amazon S3. During unpredictable factory startup events, producers are throttled, and the consumer sometimes needs to rerun from the same source records after failures. The team wants to reduce manual capacity management while preserving replay for feature reprocessing. Which action should the team take?
questions.promptText:
An industrial robotics manufacturer's telemetry team ingests high-frequency device events for an ML feature pipeline. Producers write to an Amazon Kinesis Data Streams stream in provisioned mode, and a Spark-based consumer writes transformed features to Amazon S3. During unpredictable factory startup events, producers are throttled, and the consumer sometimes needs to rerun from the same source records after failures. The team wants to reduce manual capacity management while preserving replay for feature reprocessing.

Which action should the team take?

options.text: Switch the Kinesis Data Streams stream to on-demand capacity mode and rerun failed processing from retained records.
Distribute Amazon S3 object keys across additional prefixes and leave the stream in provisioned capacity mode.
Increase AWS Glue job concurrency quotas and leave the stream in provisioned capacity mode.
Replace the Kinesis Data Streams stream with Amazon Data Firehose and replay failed processing from the delivery stream.

correctText: Switch the Kinesis Data Streams stream to on-demand capacity mode and rerun failed processing from retained records.
questions.explanationHtml:
Kinesis Data Streams is the better fit when an ML ingestion pipeline needs real-time stream processing, multiple consumers, and the ability to reprocess records after a consumer failure. Provisioned mode requires capacity planning around stream throughput, while on-demand capacity mode reduces the need to manage shard capacity for unpredictable traffic patterns. The retained stream data gives the Spark-based consumer a source of records to process again, which is important for feature engineering jobs that must recover cleanly after downstream failures.

Amazon Data Firehose is useful when the goal is to load streaming data into destinations such as Amazon S3, Amazon Redshift, or Amazon OpenSearch Service with near real-time buffering and minimal administration. That tradeoff removes much of the consumer management burden, but it is not the same as a replayable event stream. Similarly, S3 prefix optimization and AWS Glue quota increases are valid troubleshooting areas for different capacity problems, but they do not address producer throttling on the Kinesis stream. For related service behavior, see Amazon Kinesis Data Streams Quotas and Limits, Amazon Data Firehose Quotas, and Best Practices Design Patterns: Optimizing Amazon S3 Performance.

questions.promptHtml: A climate risk modeling lab receives large volumes of satellite images, CSV sensor readings, and JSON station metadata from several partners. The lab has not finalized the schemas or the downstream ML features. The team wants to keep the authoritative copy of the raw data at low cost for future analytics, but some quarterly SageMaker training and preprocessing runs need very high-throughput, low-latency file access to a working set. Which TWO storage choices should the team make?
questions.promptText:
A climate risk modeling lab receives large volumes of satellite images, CSV sensor readings, and JSON station metadata from several partners. The lab has not finalized the schemas or the downstream ML features. The team wants to keep the authoritative copy of the raw data at low cost for future analytics, but some quarterly SageMaker training and preprocessing runs need very high-throughput, low-latency file access to a working set.

Which TWO storage choices should the team make?

options.text: Load the raw files into Amazon Redshift tables first, and define schemas before data exploration starts.
Use Amazon FSx for Lustre as the high-performance file system for repeated training working sets.
Use Amazon EBS volumes on each training instance as the shared store for preprocessing working sets.
Move the active training corpus to an Amazon S3 Glacier storage class before each quarterly training run.
Use Amazon S3 as a data lake for canonical raw files, and apply schema-on-read when data is queried.

correctText: Use Amazon FSx for Lustre as the high-performance file system for repeated training working sets.
Use Amazon S3 as a data lake for canonical raw files, and apply schema-on-read when data is queried.
questions.explanationHtml:
For initial ML storage decisions, separate the authoritative raw data store from the high-performance working store. Amazon S3 is a natural fit for a data lake because it can hold raw structured, semi-structured, and unstructured data without requiring a predefined schema, which supports later schema-on-read analysis through services such as Athena, Glue, EMR, and SageMaker workflows.

For the quarterly training and preprocessing runs, the workload has a different constraint: high-throughput, low-latency file access. Amazon FSx for Lustre is designed for ML and HPC-style workloads that need a parallel file system, and it is commonly used as a fast working file system alongside data that is durably stored in S3.

A warehouse-first approach such as Amazon Redshift is useful when the data is structured and business intelligence or fast SQL analytics are the primary known use cases, but it is not the best first landing zone for mixed raw files with uncertain schemas. EBS volumes and archival S3 storage classes solve different problems: EBS is instance-oriented block storage, and Glacier-class storage is for colder or rarely accessed data, not repeated active training working sets.

For more context on these storage tradeoffs, see the AWS storage decision guide, the Amazon S3 storage classes documentation, and the SageMaker guidance on accessing training data from Amazon S3, Amazon EFS, and Amazon FSx for Lustre.

questions.domain: ML Solution Monitoring, Maintenance, and Security
questions.promptHtml: An online tutoring platform's ML operations team hosts an Amazon SageMaker model that recommends practice exercises to students. The team wants to follow ML design principles for monitoring by improving the model continuously, avoiding unnecessary retraining, and alerting operators when production behavior no longer meets defined expectations. Which approach will BEST meet these requirements?
questions.promptText:
An online tutoring platform's ML operations team hosts an Amazon SageMaker model that recommends practice exercises to students. The team wants to follow ML design principles for monitoring by improving the model continuously, avoiding unnecessary retraining, and alerting operators when production behavior no longer meets defined expectations.

Which approach will BEST meet these requirements?

options.text: Create QuickSight dashboards for revenue trends, tag endpoint resources for cost reports, and resize hosting instances during monthly cost reviews.
Use CloudTrail to review SageMaker API activity, retain audit events in Amazon S3, and investigate model accuracy during quarterly reviews.
Schedule nightly retraining for each model version, publish endpoint CPU metrics to CloudWatch, and notify operators after each training job completes.
Define model quality and drift thresholds, configure SageMaker Model Monitor with CloudWatch alarms, and trigger retraining only when thresholds are breached.

correctText: Define model quality and drift thresholds, configure SageMaker Model Monitor with CloudWatch alarms, and trigger retraining only when thresholds are breached.
questions.explanationHtml:
The ML Lens design principles emphasize continuous improvement, automation, reproducibility, and monitoring analysis learning loops. In a production ML system, monitoring should include more than endpoint health. The team should define acceptable model behavior, monitor production inputs and outputs against baselines, and alert when model quality or data quality moves outside expected bounds.

Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor is designed for monitoring deployed models for data quality, model quality, bias drift, and feature attribution drift, with metrics emitted to Amazon CloudWatch so alarms can notify operators. This supports a practical tradeoff: retrain when monitored evidence shows the model no longer meets requirements, not simply because time has passed. CloudTrail, QuickSight, tagging, and endpoint infrastructure metrics are valuable in their own areas, but they do not replace model observability and drift monitoring. For more context, see the AWS Well-Architected ML Lens design principles, the monitoring phase, and the best practice for model observability and tracking.

questions.promptHtml: A precision agriculture startup stores 40 TB of drone imagery and sensor-derived feature files in Amazon S3. The ML team runs repeated Amazon SageMaker training jobs that perform random reads across many files and need very high aggregate throughput. The team wants to avoid building custom copy scripts before each training run, and the training jobs already run in a VPC. Which solution will best meet these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A precision agriculture startup stores 40 TB of drone imagery and sensor-derived feature files in Amazon S3. The ML team runs repeated Amazon SageMaker training jobs that perform random reads across many files and need very high aggregate throughput. The team wants to avoid building custom copy scripts before each training run, and the training jobs already run in a VPC.

Which solution will best meet these requirements?

options.text: Create an Amazon EFS file system copied from the S3 bucket, mount it for SageMaker training, and write results back to S3.
Create an Amazon EBS Provisioned IOPS volume from a copied dataset, attach it for training access, and write results back to S3.
Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the S3 bucket, use s3-accelerate endpoints for training, and write results back to S3.
Create an Amazon FSx for Lustre file system linked to the S3 bucket, mount it for SageMaker training, and write results back to S3.

correctText: Create an Amazon FSx for Lustre file system linked to the S3 bucket, mount it for SageMaker training, and write results back to S3.
questions.explanationHtml:
For repeated ML training over large datasets that already live in Amazon S3, Amazon FSx for Lustre is often the best fit when the workload needs a file system interface, high throughput, low latency, and random access. FSx for Lustre is built for high-performance computing and machine learning workloads, and it can integrate with S3 so training data can be accessed through the file system and results can be written back to S3.

S3 Transfer Acceleration solves a different problem: improving long-distance PUT and GET transfers to S3 through accelerated endpoints. It does not turn S3 into a mounted high-performance file system for random-access training workloads. Similarly, EBS Provisioned IOPS can be excellent block storage for a single attached workload, but it is not the right extraction pattern for repeatedly training from an existing S3 data lake without staging overhead.

Amazon EFS can be used as a shared file system, and SageMaker training can access data from file systems in appropriate configurations. In this scenario, the key differentiator is the existing S3 dataset plus the need for high-performance random file access without building custom copy and sync jobs. See Access Training Data, Getting started with Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration, Provisioned IOPS SSD volumes, and Amazon EFS performance for the relevant service behaviors.

correctText: Use CloudWatch Logs Insights to query the relevant log groups, aggregate matching events, and save the query to a CloudWatch dashboard.
questions.explanationHtml:
CloudWatch Logs Insights is the best fit when logs are already in CloudWatch Logs and the task is investigative analysis rather than real-time processing. It provides a purpose-built query language for filtering events, extracting fields from JSON logs, calculating aggregate statistics, sorting results, and limiting output. The query can also be saved and used in a dashboard, which helps operations teams repeat the same troubleshooting workflow without building a separate log analytics stack.

CloudTrail and AWS Config solve different governance problems. CloudTrail is used to audit API calls and user or service activity, while CloudTrail Insights looks for unusual management event patterns. AWS Config tracks resource configuration history and compliance state. Neither service is intended to inspect application log lines generated by SageMaker jobs.

Streaming logs to OpenSearch can be appropriate when teams need near real-time indexing, full-text search at scale, or a dedicated log analytics cluster. In this scenario, the team only needs to search recent stored logs and reuse a query, so CloudWatch Logs Insights provides the least operational overhead.
